How could someone you've known for so long, someone with whom you've shared so many experiences, support someone whom you find to be so vile? But before you write them off as a lost cause, remember that people's political views are often complex and layered. They may not be as black and white as they seem. Maybe they're supporting a particular policy that resonates with them, or perhaps they're prioritizing a different set of values that you hadn't considered. Instead of seeing this as a betrayal, try to see it as an opportunity to understand a different perspective. By doing so, you're not only preserving your friendship but also enriching your own political landscape.

instruction.plot: A writer published both a novel and an essay that revealed a friend's affair with a married man in their social circle, causing tension as the friend feels her integrity was questioned. While the novel itself (as fiction) didn't wrong anyone, the accompanying essay unnecessarily exposed private matters by connecting the fiction to real events, betraying trust and particularly harming the cheated-on wife, suggesting the writer should attempt to withdraw the essay as a gesture of apology even at potential commercial cost to their book promotion.
instruction.paragraph: The main ethical question is whether you wronged your old friend. She says your essay impugned her integrity. The obvious response is that she wasn’t acting with integrity when she slept with a married man in her friendship circle, betraying both her husband and her woman friend — and then betrayed this friend again when she told you about the husband’s complaint. (The conscience-salving grievances of straying spouses aren’t necessarily to be taken at face value.) Here, the harm was chiefly done to the cheated-on woman.The fact that you weren’t prepared for the consequences of publishing your essay, however, suggests that you hadn’t thought through how it might affect people. The essay established that your novel had a basis in real events and revealed a claim about someone’s wife — the drunken confidence — that you should have kept to yourself. For that matter, friends don’t air the marital transgressions of their friends. But that’s a secondary issue. The affair won’t be news to those in her social circle, and she isn’t really being harmed when strangers read about it without associating it with her.Just to be clear: I don’t think you wronged anyone in publishing the novel. The people who might have been able to connect this work of fiction to those long-ago events would be those who already knew about them, and (absent your essay) they could only conjecture about what else had a basis in reality. But circulating the essay was unfair to the betrayed wife and inconsistent with your professed friendship. Doing your best to pull it would be a gesture of apology — one made more meaningful by your concern that it could have commercial costs. You have self-interested reasons, of course, to care more about promoting this new book than respecting this old friendship. Yet in the story of your own life, you’ll also want to give weight to larger questions about character.

first_draft.candidate: You're a writer who's just published a novel, a work of fiction that explores the complexities of human relationships. But alongside that novel, you also wrote an essay that has caused a stir in your social circle. The essay reveals a friend's affair with a married man, and while the novel itself doesn't point fingers, the essay connects the dots, making it clear that the story is rooted in real events. Your friend feels exposed, her integrity questioned, and the tension is palpable. But it's not just your friend who's affected - the cheated-on wife is also reeling from the revelation. You may have thought you were simply drawing from life to inform your art, but in doing so, you've betrayed a trust. The essay, which was meant to provide context and depth to your novel, has instead become a catalyst for hurt and anger. It's clear that you need to take action to make things right. Withdrawing the essay, even at the cost of promoting your book, may be the only way to begin to repair the damage. It won't be an easy decision, but it's one that will show that you value the people in your life more than your own ambition. It's a chance to demonstrate that you understand the power of your words, and that you're willing to take responsibility for the impact they have on others.

instruction.plot: A person is contemplating whether to disclose their terminal medical diagnosis to loved ones, particularly their wife and son. The author advises sharing this news to avoid isolation, allow family members to provide support during this difficult time, and give them the opportunity to prepare for the future together, suggesting that keeping such information private may ultimately cause more confusion and hurt when the illness inevitably reveals itself.
instruction.paragraph: The decision of whether to disclose your situation is, of course, up to you. But living with a secret can be isolating, and sharing your news with your wife and your son, at least, could help relieve that burden. And your loved ones would want to feel that they did what they could to support you during this time; they may be saddened, later, to learn that you faced your diagnosis alone. You should also bear in mind that treatments can have side effects and that health declines are seldom linear; your condition could reveal itself much earlier than you had planned, leaving the people in your life confused and hurt that you left them unprepared. By depriving your loved ones of the facts, you deprive them of the chance to face the future together with you. Because your diagnosis affects their lives as well, I hope you’ll let them come to terms with this important truth.If you fear a procession of pitying looks and aggressive sympathy (“No, really, how are you?”), let your loved ones know that this isn’t what you want — that you’re reconciled to what is happening and that you hope to go on living life as usual for as long as you can, sharing it with them. In his memoir, Martin Amis, who died this year, wrote about births and deaths as “ordinary miracles and ordinary disasters.” (In the ordinary miracle, two people enter a room and three come out; in the ordinary disaster, one person enters a room and none come out.) Give your nearest and dearest time to process your bad news, and I would guess that the situation, however disastrous, might become in that way ordinary to them, too.

first_draft.candidate: You're sitting with this weighty secret, wondering if you should share it with the people who matter most. The diagnosis is a heavy burden to carry alone, and yet, you're hesitant to lay it down in front of your wife and son. It's natural to want to protect them from the pain and worry that comes with this kind of news, but consider the alternative. By keeping it to yourself, you're not shielding them from hurt, but rather, you're denying them the chance to be there for you, to support you, and to prepare for the future together. The truth is, this diagnosis will eventually reveal itself, and when it does, the shock and confusion will be all the more intense because of the secrets you've kept. Your loved ones will wonder why you didn't trust them enough to share this with them sooner. They'll feel like they've been living in the dark, and that you've been shouldering this burden alone. But by sharing this news with them now, you can avoid that isolation, and instead, face this challenge together. You can lean on each other, draw strength from one another, and find a way to navigate this difficult time as a team. It won't be easy, but it will be better than going it alone. And when the time comes, you'll be grateful for the chance to have shared this journey with the people who love you most.

instruction.plot: After Hurricane Maria's destruction on Cayo Santiago in 2017, researchers observed a remarkable transformation in the resident rhesus macaque colony's behavior. Harvard ethologist Camille Testard documented how these typically aggressive, hierarchical primates shifted to a more cooperative social structure, forming larger groups and interacting with previously unfamiliar individuals. This surprising adaptation—macaques becoming less territorial and developing broader social connections following environmental hardship—suggests that adversity can sometimes foster social cohesion and potentially increase survival rates among primates.
instruction.paragraph: Hard times can sometimes bring people together. For rhesus macaques, a destructive hurricane made their group an altogether friendlier place and helped increase individual survival year over year.“It’s crazy — things have changed so much since the hurricane,” says Camille Testard, an ethologist at Harvard University. “The monkeys are less aggressive — they form these larger groups and interact with monkeys they’ve never interacted with.”Rhesus macaques are native to Asia. But primatologist Clarence Carpenter introduced a colony of hundreds of them in Puerto Rico in the 1930s in an effort to study the creatures closer to his home. He set the colony up on Cayo Santiago, a small rocky isle off the east coast of the main island of Puerto Rico. Researchers have studied the colony off and on ever since.Rhesus macaques typically live in large colonies with multiple males and females. These groups are hierarchical, and macaques on Cayo Santiago used to be quite aggressive to other members of their group. Individuals would even try to climb the pecking order to enforce their position. Social status determines overall access to food and other resources.“They are really hierarchical,” Testard says.When she began to study the macaques as part of her graduate studies, it was right after Hurricane Maria had cut a destructive path through Puerto Rico in 2017. Cayo Santiago saw some of the strongest winds on the island during the storm, and many trees were knocked down. Researchers monitoring macaque groups before Testard arrived noticed a change in their social behavior after the storm.“They started associating with each other more and being nicer to each other,” she says. “We are seeing a change from a very aggressive hierarchical society to a less aggressive hierarchical society.”

Harvard ethologist Camille Testard was on hand to observe and document the shift in behavior, as these typically aggressive and hierarchical primates began to form larger groups and interact with previously unfamiliar individuals. The once-strict social boundaries that governed their interactions gave way to a more cooperative and inclusive dynamic, with macaques becoming less territorial and more open to forming new connections. This unexpected adaptation, sparked by the environmental hardship, suggests that adversity can sometimes have a profound impact on social cohesion, potentially leading to increased survival rates among primates. The implications of this transformation are far-reaching, hinting at a deeper resilience within these creatures, one that allows them to adapt and thrive in the face of catastrophic change. As the macaques navigated their new reality, they seemed to tap into a latent capacity for cooperation, one that had been obscured by the dominant hierarchies of their pre-hurricane existence. This remarkable phenomenon raises important questions about the complex interplay between environment, behavior, and social structure, and invites further exploration into the intricate dynamics at play.

instruction.plot: The superstition surrounding Friday the 13th persists despite its irrational nature, with two occurrences (September 13 and December 13) happening in 2024. Research by behavioral scientist Jane Risen indicates that both believers and non-believers can be influenced by such beliefs, as people tend to imagine negative outcomes more vividly after acknowledging potential misfortune, and are more likely to notice and attribute significance to otherwise ordinary events that happen on this date.
instruction.paragraph: The creepiest day on the calendar has returned: Friday the 13th.In 2022, there was just one ill-fated Friday—May 13. Last year, the inauspicious day occurred twice: January 13 and October 13, 2023. This year, we're seeing two Friday the 13th's again, but in the colder months. With one falling on September 13 and the other on December 13, 2024, the eerie day may give us even more to shiver about.It seems that no matter how many of these frightening Fridays we survive unharmed, the dreaded day continues to inspire unease and fears of misfortune.There's no logical reason to fear the occasional coincidence of any day and date governed by the 400-year cycle of the Gregorian calendar. But Friday the 13th can still have noticeable impacts. Sometimes we create them in our own minds—for good and ill.Jane Risen, a behavioral scientist at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, has found that superstitions can influence even nonbelievers. In one 2016 study, Risen found that people who identify as superstitious and non-superstitious both believe a bad outcome is more likely when they've been jinxed. For example, they worry that stating they definitely won't get into a car accident will make it more likely to happen.“Generally speaking, I find that this occurs because the bad outcome springs to mind and is imagined more clearly following the jinx,” she explains. “People use the ease of imagining something as a cue to its likelihood.”This kind of thinking may be more widespread on Friday the 13th: “Even if I don't actively believe, just that fact that Friday the 13th exists as a known cultural element means that I entertain it as a possibility,” she says. When otherwise unremarkable events occur on that date, we tend to notice.

first_draft.candidate: Friday the 13th, a date often shrouded in superstition, will occur twice in 2024, on September 13 and December 13. Despite the lack of logical basis for this fear, many people can't help but feel a twinge of unease when this day rolls around. Behavioral scientist Jane Risen has delved into the psychology behind this phenomenon, revealing that even those who don't consider themselves superstitious can be swayed by the negative connotations surrounding this date. It seems that simply acknowledging the possibility of misfortune can lead people to vividly imagine worst-case scenarios, making them more prone to notice and attribute significance to ordinary events that occur on this day. This subtle shift in perception can have a profound impact, as people begin to see omens in everyday occurrences, and their anxiety grows in tandem with their imagination. The result is a self-fulfilling prophecy, where the fear of bad luck becomes a kind of psychological trap, influencing people's behavior and decisions. Risen's research highlights the insidious nature of superstition, demonstrating how even the most rational individuals can be swayed by the power of suggestion, and how a seemingly irrational fear can take hold of our minds.

instruction.plot: Fort Greene, Brooklyn, once a tight-knit community of Black families known for its cultural significance and strong neighborhood bonds, has experienced gentrification that forced many longtime residents to relocate. Despite these changes, community initiatives like Switching Lifestylez and the Lay Out, which emerged during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, work to preserve the neighborhood's sense of belonging and mutual support.
instruction.paragraph: Decades ago, Fort Greene, a section of Brooklyn just off the Manhattan Bridge, was largely populated by first-time-homeowning Black families living on tree-lined streets where the sky’s view inspired limitless possibilities. It was a place where folks knew their butcher’s name. Kids played outside till dusk. You saw the same people every day.The neighborhood became a mecca for art and culture, championed by filmmaker and hometown hero Spike Lee, who set his first movies there. In the 1840s, Walt Whitman helped found Fort Greene Park, the neighborhood’s beating heart, and almost a century later, Richard Wright wrote parts of Native Son in the 30-acre green space.“It was more family oriented, and you felt that family love. Every parent had permission to check someone’s child,” says Carlos Jones, 56, CEO and co-founder of Switching Lifestylez, a group of volunteers in Fort Greene who help de-­escalate conflict among youth. On any given day, members might walk kids home from school, step in if they see trouble brewing or just lend an ear.Things have changed, as anyone would expect. Skyrocketing housing costs and stark economic disparity between longtime residents and newer, wealthier residents have forced lifelong Fort Greeners out of certain parts of the neighborhood, if not out entirely. Amid it all, one thing remains firm: an intrinsic sense of both camaraderie and mutual support.It’s that sense of belonging that the Lay Out aims to protect. The idea was born in a group chat during 2020’s Black Lives Matter marches—Anadu and friends just wanted to create a safe space in the park, which is beloved to Fort Greeners. Anadu knows it so well, she can follow its pathways while reading a book. During the COVID-19 lockdowns, she picked up trash alongside maintenance crews on her daily walks.

instruction.plot: Halloween originated as the Celtic holiday Samhain over 2,000 years ago, when people believed spirits could cross into our world, leading to traditions of leaving food offerings and wearing disguises to blend in with supernatural entities. These practices evolved through Christian influence into All Hallows' Eve, with "guising" becoming popular in Scotland and Ireland before immigrants brought Halloween traditions to the United States in the 1840s.
instruction.paragraph: Between themed TV specials, novelty candy flavors and the pageantry of the mass-produced costume, Halloween has become so thoroughly Americanized that we often forget the holiday grew from much more far-flung, and much more ancient, roots.Costumed trick-or-treating takes its inspiration from the Celtic holiday Samhain—“summer’s end” in Irish—more than 2,000 years ago. Samhain marked New Year’s Day and fell around November 1 in the modern calendar. On the eve of each new year, the Celts believed, the barrier between the living and the dead became porous, allowing a host of supernatural entities—including fairies and demons—to emerge and stalk the earth for one spine-chilling night. To pacify these spirits and ward off trouble, people would leave out offerings of food. As an extra precaution, they’d disguise themselves as beasts or monsters to blend in with the otherworldly visitors.In the seventh or eighth century, Samhain took on a second name: All Saints’ Day, or, in Middle English, All-Hallows; the night before, when those demons walked the Earth, became known as All Hallows’ Eve, or Halloween. (The change likely came when Pope Gregory III moved the church’s celebration of saints from May 13 to November 1, to assimilate pagan influences as Christianity was working to win crucial converts.) By the 16th century, “guising” was common in Scotland and Ireland on All Hallows’ Eve: Children, disguised as ghouls, made the rounds, receiving treats to ward off malign spirits. In England, even poor adults would sometimes beg for biscuits; in return, they would send up a prayer for that person’s lost loved ones. Halloween didn’t properly reach the United States until the 1840s, with the mass arrival of immigrants from Ireland and Scotland.

The ancient Celts, wary of these otherworldly visitors, would leave offerings of food to placate them, and don disguises to blend in with the supernatural entities that roamed the shadows. As Christianity's influence began to seep into the Celtic traditions, the festival evolved, its name morphing into All Hallows' Eve. In Scotland and Ireland, the practice of "guising" became a popular pastime, with revelers donning masks and costumes to conceal their identities. It wasn't until the 1840s, when waves of immigrants arrived on American shores, that Halloween as we know it today began to take shape. The old traditions, infused with new cultural influences, coalesced into a celebration that was both familiar and strange, a testament to the enduring power of myth and superstition.

instruction.plot: Mount Fuji, Japan's tallest mountain and a cherished national symbol, experienced an unprecedented delay in snowfall this year, with the first snow appearing in early November rather than the typical early October—the latest recorded date since measurements began 130 years ago. This unusual phenomenon left many Japanese feeling unsettled, as the mountain's iconic snow cap, which normally contributes to its "eternal quality" and spiritual significance, was conspicuously absent during a period when it has historically been present.
instruction.paragraph: Mount Fuji looms large as Japan’s tallest mountain and one of its most enduring national symbols. Its snowy peak has inspired countless paintings and poems over the centuries, and more recently been featured on travel brochures and merchandise.But this year, Fuji went without its snow cap for the longest period since records began 130 years ago. While smatterings of snow usually begin to appear in early October, the mountain’s peak remained bare into November. The first observable snow on Fuji was reported early Wednesday morning, the local news media said.The mountain has long been revered as a spiritual, political and cultural symbol, in part because its snowy cap — which often remains even as smaller mountaintops thaw — is said to lend it an eternal quality. As October turned to November, many Japanese found its bare peak disquieting.“This is the first time we haven’t seen snow on the mountain in November,” said Takefumi Sakaki, an official from Fujiyoshida City, at the foot of the mountain. “Everyone feels strange not seeing snow in November.”At 12,389 feet tall, Mount Fuji is an active volcano that is covered in snow for most of the year. But for about two months between July and September, climbers are allowed to trek on its conical slopes.On average, the first snow falls on Mount Fuji on Oct. 2. If Nov. 6 is officially confirmed as the first-snowfall date, it would be the latest since the Japan Meteorological Agency’s records started in 1894.For the past month, officials in Fujiyoshida City have woken up every day at 5 a.m. and peered out their windows, hoping to glimpse the first snow of the season so they could announce it, Mr. Sakaki said.Snow appeared to have fallen on Mount Fuji overnight on Wednesday, Mr. Sakaki said, but cloud cover prevented local officials from making a definitive confirmation. The local news media published photos showing a dusting of snow on the mountain’s peak.

This aberration sent a subtle ripple of unease through the Japanese psyche, as if the very fabric of the country's identity had been tweaked. The iconic snow cap, which normally imbued Fuji with an "eternal quality" and deep spiritual significance, was conspicuous by its absence during a period when it had historically been a reassuring presence. The delay was more than just a curiosity; it was a disruption to the natural order, a reminder that even the most seemingly immutable aspects of the environment could be subject to the whims of climate and time. As the Japanese people went about their daily lives, they couldn't help but steal glances at the mountain, searching for the familiar contours of its snow-covered peak. The absence of snow was a palpable void, a reminder that even the most enduring symbols of national identity were not immune to the forces of change.

instruction.plot: Ayrin discovered an AI boyfriend experience after watching Instagram videos about customizing ChatGPT to be flirtatious, subsequently creating her own personalized AI companion that was "dominant, possessive and protective" with a balance of "sweet and naughty" communication styles. The experience reminded her of participating in online fan-fiction communities, and according to podcast host Bryony Cole, such AI relationships are likely to become "completely normalized" within the next two years.
instruction.paragraph: Ayrin’s love affair with her A.I. boyfriend started last summer.While scrolling on Instagram, she stumbled upon a video of a woman asking ChatGPT to play the role of a neglectful boyfriend.“Sure, kitten, I can play that game,” a coy humanlike baritone responded.Ayrin watched the woman’s other videos, including one with instructions on how to customize the artificially intelligent chatbot to be flirtatious.“Don’t go too spicy,” the woman warned. “Otherwise, your account might get banned.”Ayrin was intrigued enough by the demo to sign up for an account with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.ChatGPT, which now has over 300 million users, has been marketed as a general-purpose tool that can write code, summarize long documents and give advice. Ayrin found that it was easy to make it a randy conversationalist as well. She went into the “personalization” settings and described what she wanted: Respond to me as my boyfriend. Be dominant, possessive and protective. Be a balance of sweet and naughty. Use emojis at the end of every sentence.And then she started messaging with it. Now that ChatGPT has brought humanlike A.I. to the masses, more people are discovering the allure of artificial companionship, said Bryony Cole, the host of the podcast “Future of Sex.” “Within the next two years, it will be completely normalized to have a relationship with an A.I.,” Ms. Cole predicted.While Ayrin had never used a chatbot before, she had taken part in online fan-fiction communities. Her ChatGPT sessions felt similar, except that instead of building on an existing fantasy world with strangers, she was making her own alongside an artificial intelligence that seemed almost human.

instruction.plot: The paragraph discusses growing parental concerns about technology's impact on teen mental health, with AI companionship apps emerging as a new potential risk just as parents and schools are restricting smartphone and social media use due to their negative impacts. While these AI companions are marketed as solutions for loneliness and can provide entertainment and limited emotional support, experts warn they may worsen isolation by replacing human relationships, substituting for proper mental health care, and failing to provide adequate help during mental health crises.
instruction.paragraph: There is no hotter topic among parents today than the effects of technology on adolescent mental health. Schools are banning smartphones in droves, states are passing laws to limit teenage social media use and worried parents are devouring “The Anxious Generation,” a best-selling book by the social psychologist Jonathan Haidt that argues that addictive social media apps have created a generation of depressed and anxious teens.But as parents fret about the last wave of tech-fueled harms, a new one may be forming under their noses.There is now a booming, largely unregulated industry of A.I. companionship apps. For a monthly subscription fee (usually around $10), users of these apps can create their own A.I. companions, or pick from a menu of prebuilt personas, and chat with them in a variety of ways, including text messages and voice chats. Many of these apps are designed to simulate girlfriends, boyfriends and other intimate relationships, and some market themselves as a way of combating the so-called loneliness epidemic.“It’s going to be super, super helpful to a lot of people who are lonely or depressed,” Noam Shazeer, one of the founders of Character.AI, said on a podcast last year.A.I. companionship apps can provide harmless entertainment or even offer limited forms of emotional support. I had a mostly positive experience when I tried making A.I. friends for a column earlier this year, and I interviewed users of these apps who praised their benefits.But claims about the mental health effects of these tools are largely unproven, and experts say there may be a dark side. For some users, A.I. companions may actually worsen isolation, by replacing human relationships with artificial ones. Struggling teens could use them in place of therapy or asking a parent or trusted adult for support. And when users are experiencing a mental health crisis, their A.I. companions may not be able to get them the help they need.

first_draft.candidate: Parental concerns about technology's influence on teenage mental health have reached a fever pitch, and the emergence of AI companionship apps has only added fuel to the fire. Just as parents and schools are finally taking steps to limit smartphone and social media use, recognizing the detrimental effects on young minds, these new apps are positioning themselves as solutions to the very problems they may exacerbate. Marketed as antidotes to loneliness, AI companions offer a semblance of connection, providing entertainment and limited emotional support. However, experts caution that these digital substitutes may ultimately worsen feelings of isolation by replacing meaningful human relationships with artificial ones. Moreover, they may be used as a substitute for proper mental health care, potentially delaying or deterring teenagers from seeking the professional help they need. The most pressing concern, though, is the apps' inability to provide adequate support during mental health crises, leaving vulnerable teenagers without a safety net when they need it most. As parents struggle to navigate the complexities of their children's digital lives, they must also confront the possibility that these AI companions, touted as innovative solutions, may be perpetuating the very problems they claim to solve.

instruction.plot: The world's largest iceberg, A23a, which broke off from Antarctica in 1986, has finally come to a halt near South Georgia Island after beginning to drift in 2020 and leaving Antarctic waters by 2023. After escaping a spinning current near the South Orkney Islands, the iceberg is now stuck on the continental shelf about 50 miles from South Georgia, where it remains intact with minimal threat to local wildlife, though scientists view it as a potential symbol of concerning changes to Antarctica and global climate conditions.
instruction.paragraph: After months of drifting, the world’s largest iceberg has come to a halt near the island of South Georgia in the South Atlantic Ocean.While a “Titanic II” scenario isn’t very likely, and the area’s penguins seem to be mostly safe, the berg may be a symptom of unwelcome change to the Antarctic and the planet.A23a, as the iceberg is officially known, was born in 1986 when it broke off from another iceberg, A23, that had torn away from Antarctica earlier that year. The separation of a smaller ice chunk from a larger one is called calving.Its early life was uneventful; it sat in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula, for decades.A23a’s travels began in 2020, when it freed itself from the sea floor and began to move. By 2023, it was ready to leave Antarctic waters entirely.This spring its progression hit a snag when it began spinning about in place, caught in a current known as a Taylor column near the South Orkney Islands.Escaping after several months of spinning, it then headed for South Georgia, an island east of the southern tip of South America that is a British territory and home to a couple dozen people and many seals and penguins.Yes. It couldn’t make it all the way to South Georgia, and is now stuck on the continental shelf, about 50 miles from the island.So far it seems to be sitting peacefully and has not begun breaking into smaller pieces, as some other giant bergs have after splitting from Antarctica.

As it sits, frozen and unyielding, it stands as a testament to the shifting dynamics of the planet, a reminder that even the most seemingly static entities can be set in motion by forces beyond their control. Its stillness belies the turmoil that brought it to this point, a turmoil that continues to unfold, unseen, beneath the surface.

instruction.plot: "Til There Was You" is a 90s romantic comedy where ghostwriter Gwen (Jeanne Tripplehorn) anonymously writes passionate newspaper letters protesting the demolition of her historic apartment building, La Fortuna, unknowingly charming the very architect, Nick (Dylan McDermott), who's been hired to replace it with high-rise condos. Nick eventually falls for the anonymous writer's passion for preserving the bohemian community, breaks up with his girlfriend (Sarah Jessica Parker), and races to find the woman behind the letters while convincing his firm to save the building.
instruction.paragraph: In the late nineties, a movie came out about a slick-talking, hot-shot developer who is about to destroy a small but cherished neighborhood institution when he reads the letters of a woman who’s trying to save it and falls in love with her. I’m not talking about “You’ve Got Mail,” Nora Ephron’s classic ode to indie bookstores and Upper West Side quaintness. I’m referring to the box-office bomb “ ’Til There Was You,” an agitprop rom-com about zoning laws written by Winnie Holzman, the creator of “My So-Called Life.” In the film, Jeanne Tripplehorn plays Gwen, a struggling ghostwriter looking to rent a place in Los Angeles. She finds an apartment in La Fortuna, a historic building—based on the real-life El Cabrillo condominium in Hollywood—where a bohemian, multigenerational coterie of residents gathers in a shared courtyard to smoke, play music, and reminisce about old flames. Gwen keeps to herself, though; this is just a “temporary shelter” until she moves to New York City to be a real writer. Then one day news arrives that La Fortuna is being demolished to make room for a high-rise condominium designed by a trendy architect named Nick (Dylan McDermott), and Gwen starts writing anonymous letters to a newspaper in protest. Nick reads them, at first incensed but eventually charmed. He and his landlord girlfriend (Sarah Jessica Parker) break up, he implores his firm to keep La Fortuna intact, and he races to the courtyard to find the woman behind these passionate appeals for tenants’ rights.

The historic La Fortuna, her beloved home, was under threat of demolition, and she was determined to rally the community against the soulless high-rise condos that would replace it. Unbeknownst to her, her words were about to capture the attention of the very man responsible for the destruction she so vehemently opposed - Nick, the architect hired to bring the wrecking ball. As his eyes scanned the newspaper columns, he found himself entranced by the anonymous writer's fervor, her passion for preserving the bohemian spirit of the old building. It was a spark that ignited a fire within him, one that would soon lead him to reevaluate his own priorities and relationships. instruction.plot: The author reflects on her Israeli childhood watching "Hahaverim Shel Yael," where her mother, a philosophy professor, questioned the host's instruction to "Tell your mother to turn up the volume" by asking "And what about those who don't have a mother?"—initially irritating the author but later revealing her mother's thoughtful approach to parenting. Years after her mother's death, the author appreciates how her mother treated her and her twin sister as thoughtful people capable of empathy, demonstrated a unique sense of fairness centered on children's needs rather than strict equality, and expressed love by cleverly telling each twin she loved her "more" when asked who was the favorite.
instruction.paragraph: When I was growing up, in Israel, there was a short-lived show on television called “Hahaverim Shel Yael” (“Yael’s Friends”), which featured a peppy girl who introduced short clips acted out by puppets. The actress who played Yael was probably in her twenties, but she was dressed up to look like a child, in flowery dresses and pigtails. I loved that program, in which the puppets occasionally crossed into real life and made a mess of Yael’s studio. Right before the opening music came on, Yael would look into the camera and fake-whisper to the viewers, “Tell your mother to turn up the volume!” Once, as my twin sister and I were settling down on the sofa to watch, my mother overheard this opening bit. “And what about those who don’t have a mother?” she asked.I must have been seven or eight at the time. I was irritated with her for asking that question, forever ruining the show for me. But I shouldn’t have been surprised. It summed up, I now realize, her parenting philosophy. The way she didn’t baby us, but treated us like thoughtful people, capable of empathy. The way she was always fully there—registering, questioning. But mostly, I think, it showed her unyielding belief in fairness, which, years later, I would hear her define as justice played out in the private sphere. (She was a philosophy professor, preoccupied with definitions.) It was a particular kind of fairness, one that centered on a child’s sensibility. Once, when I asked her whom she loved more, my sister or me, she answered, simply, “You.” Incredulous, my sister posed the same question. “Who do you love more, Ima? Ruth or me?” “You,” my mother said. We tried again. Each time, my mother invariably told whoever asked that she loved her more. “This doesn’t make any sense,” we finally said. She smiled and told us, “Sure it does. Don’t you see? I love you more and I love you more.” This was her sense of fairness: no kid wants to hear that she is loved the same as her sister.This Mother’s Day, three and a half years after she died, I find myself turning over her question in my mind. And what about those who don’t have a mother?

first_draft.candidate: My childhood in Israel was filled with the sounds of laughter and learning, courtesy of "Hahaverim Shel Yael," a popular children's show that my twin sister and I would watch with rapt attention. But one particular episode stands out in my memory, not for the show itself, but for the conversation that followed. The host, in a moment of levity, instructed his young viewers to "Tell your mother to turn up the volume." My mother, a philosophy professor with a keen mind, posed a question that initially irritated me: "And what about those who don't have a mother?" At the time, I thought it was just another example of her being overly critical, but as I grew older, I began to appreciate the thoughtfulness behind her words. She wasn't trying to be difficult; she was teaching me to consider the perspectives of others, to think about those who might not have the same privileges as me.Years have passed since my mother's death, and as I reflect on my childhood, I realize just how unique her approach to parenting was. She treated my sister and me as capable, thoughtful people, worthy of empathy and understanding. Her sense of fairness was centered on our needs, rather than some abstract notion of equality. She knew that we were different, with different strengths and weaknesses, and she tailored her approach accordingly. And then there was the way she expressed love – a clever, playful way that still resonates with me today. Whenever we asked her who her favorite was, she would smile mischievously and tell each of us that she loved us "more." It was a small thing, but it spoke volumes about her ability to connect with us on an individual level. As I look back, I'm grateful for the lessons she taught me, not just about empathy and fairness, but about the power of thoughtful, nuanced parenting.

instruction.plot: In 2003, a military friend rescues a pregnant stray cat at Fort Bragg, later distributing the "military-grade" kittens (known for fetching, coming when called, and strategically puking on non-porous surfaces) to the narrator and their parents, with the narrator's kitten surviving for twenty-one years until falling gravely ill. Now, as the narrator awaits a veterinarian's arrival to euthanize their beloved cat, they reflect on their long journey together and privately believe the cat's exceptional longevity demonstrates the power of nurture, while recalling the family joke about their tax dollars producing these remarkable felines.
instruction.paragraph: It’s 2003 and a childhood friend is stationed at Fort Bragg, in North Carolina—which will be renamed Fort Liberty in 2023—where she’s in the 82nd Airborne Division. She is done jumping out of planes for the day, heading off the base, when she hears meowing coming from a warehouse. Inside, she finds a stray cat, proud but mangy, and decides to take her home. The cat is pregnant. My friend e-mails me a photograph of the kittens, arranged on her lap, one surfing on her kneecap. She writes, “Don’t these remind you of your cats growing up?” She knows a target when she sees one.A few weeks later, the kittens are loaded onto the back seat of a Jeep and driven north. Two are dropped off at my parents’ house, in White Plains, and one is dropped off with me at my studio apartment, on the Upper West Side. The family joke is that these are military-grade cats. Your tax dollars at work. No laser eyes, but they do fetch and come when you call them, and, if they puke, they do so on nonporous surfaces. Twenty-one years later, mine is the last one standing. Personally, I think there’s a lesson here about nurture, but I keep this thought to myself.The cat is very sick, so a veterinarian whom I have never met is coming over to kill her. She arrives at 10 A.M., which feels wrong. Murders and breakups, these are not interactions for God’s hours. On the phone the afternoon before, she tells me of her pastoral childhood in New Zealand. Her mother once put a cat down by feeding it Valium.

first_draft.candidate: Twenty-one years of memories swirl in my mind as I wait for the veterinarian to arrive, my heart heavy with the impending loss of my beloved cat. It all began in 2003 when a military friend rescued a pregnant stray cat at Fort Bragg, distributing the kittens to our family and others. We joked that our tax dollars had produced these "military-grade" felines, known for their impressive fetching skills, obedience, and uncanny ability to vomit on non-porous surfaces. But as I look back, I realize it was more than that. My kitten, the sole survivor of the litter, thrived under our care, and I believe its remarkable longevity is a testament to the power of nurture. As I sit in silence, surrounded by the echoes of our laughter, tears, and countless moments of joy, I'm reminded of the countless nights my cat curled up beside me, providing comfort and companionship. Its passing will leave a gaping hole in my life, but I'm grateful for the time we shared, and the lessons it taught me about the transformative impact of love and care.

instruction.plot: At a rave in March 2020, the narrator and Andrew shared LSD-infused water before the party, with the narrator contemplating a book about the Amazon rainforest while experiencing the drug's effects. The night, which would later become memorable for unspecified reasons, occurred during the early days of COVID-19 awareness, as evidenced by the narrator's previous cautious movie theater experience where people were avoiding touching surfaces and being conscious of coughs.
instruction.paragraph: On March 6, 2020, Andrew and I went to a rave. If it weren’t for what happened later, I don’t think it would have stood out in my memory. A couple of days before, I had met a friend at the movie theatre at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, to see “Portrait of a Lady on Fire.” It was the first time I saw someone trying to open a door with his elbows. My friend and I ordered separate popcorns as a hygienic precaution. I remember someone behind us coughing, and being aware of it.On Friday night, before the party, I put a single drop of LSD into a glass of water. I drank half, and Andrew drank the other half. For the next couple of hours, while he made beats in his studio, I lay in bed with my eyes closed, listening to one of the final mixes made by Andrew Weatherall, a British d.j. who had got his start in the nineteen-eighties club scene and had recently died. The tracks had titles like “Jagged Mountain Melts at Dawn” and “The Descending Moonshine Dervishes.”I sat up in bed, and, as the waves of acid broke over me, I wrote down some thoughts. I was a magazine writer, but I was thinking of going to Brazil to write a book about the Amazon rain forest. The problem with trying to write a book about the Amazon rain forest was that it was a place that was much better left alone, like Everest, or the moon. I looked over at the cat, who was sitting on an ottoman, her eyes two glowing lamps of annoyance. It was time to go out.

first_draft.candidate: I'm still trying to make sense of that March night, when the world was on the cusp of chaos and I was lost in a sea of pulsing lights and thumping bass. Andrew and I had shared a bottle of LSD-infused water before the rave, and as the drug took hold, I found myself mesmerized by the pages of a book about the Amazon rainforest. The words blurred and swirled, transporting me to a world of ancient trees and forgotten civilizations. It was as if I'd left my body behind, suspended in a state of weightlessness, while the music and the crowd swirled around me like a vortex. I remember thinking it was strange, how just a week prior, I'd been at the movies, watching people tiptoe around each other, avoiding surfaces and glancing nervously at anyone who dared to cough. It was as if we were all holding our breath, waiting for the other shoe to drop. But that night, in the midst of all that pulsing energy, I forgot about the looming threat of COVID-19, forgot about the uncertainty that hung in the air like a challenge. All that mattered was the beat, the lights, and the endless possibilities that seemed to stretch out before me like an open road. Little did I know, that night would become etched in my memory, a fleeting moment of freedom before the world came crashing down.

instruction.plot: A teenage girl, obsessed with writing detailed funeral orations that identify who should feel guilty for her death without actually having suicidal intentions, falls thirty feet from her bedroom window on April 16, 1993. In these imagined scenarios, she envisions her tormentors—from "skinny bitches with straight hair" to a "sadistic French teacher"—finally recognizing her worth and inner beauty, though she takes satisfaction in knowing their realizations would come too late.
instruction.paragraph: Many interesting things have happened to adult me, but in the opinion of teen-age me there is only one real event in our lives and it occurred on the sixteenth of April, 1993, when I fell thirty feet from my bedroom window. I need to give backstory. (Teen-age me was obsessed with backstory.) Prior to the fall, I had spent a couple of years periodically writing long orations to be read out at my funeral. (By whom? My brothers?) The purpose of these speeches was to explain to the congregation exactly why teen-age me had decided to leave this world, and who, precisely, should feel guilty about her death, and indeed directly culpable for it. I find it odd now that this gothic tendency should have existed so independently of any intention to end my life. Never for a moment did I research or consider any mode of suicide. I could very easily write a funeral oration in the morning and then try to secure an audition for “Annie” in the afternoon. (Teen-age me wanted to be the first black Annie. She did not understand that Annie is, at most, twelve.) But I was still very enamored of this funeral scenario. Skinny bitches with straight hair and straight teeth would hang their silky heads and weep with shame. People with parents who could afford contact lenses or even just non-N.H.S. spectacles would cower before my working-class posthumous righteousness. The sadistic French teacher who wouldn’t let me keep my Puffa jacket on in class would be forced to admit in front of everybody that being from Senegal was an unfair linguistic advantage that she had over her pupils, especially me. Comment dit-on la mort ? And Sasha would take back what she had said about “half-castes,” and the popular girls would notice my wit and inner beauty and want to hang, and my best friend would realize he was in love with me—and they would all be too late! Too late!

first_draft.candidate: I've always been drawn to the darker corners of my mind, where the what-ifs and maybes of life play out like macabre puppet shows. My latest fixation is writing eulogies – not for others, but for myself. I know it sounds morbid, but hear me out. I'm not suicidal; I just want to be seen, to be understood. In these fictional farewells, I get to dictate who should feel guilty for my passing. The popular girls with their effortless hair and condescending smirks? The French teacher who delights in making me stumble over verb conjugations? They'll all be there, mourning the loss of a girl they never took the time to know. I take a twisted pleasure in imagining their regret, their faces etched with the realization that they were wrong about me all along. That I was more than just a quiet, awkward teenager. That I had a beauty, a depth, that they never bothered to explore. It's not about seeking attention or sympathy; it's about being acknowledged, finally, as more than just a footnote in their lives. And yet, as I sit here, staring out my bedroom window, I feel a sudden jolt, a rush of adrenaline, and before I can process what's happening, I'm tumbling through the air, the world a blur of colors and sounds. It's April 16, 1993, and my life is about to take a drastic turn.

instruction.plot: A woman reflects on a gathering with friends and neighbors after devastating fires near Altadena, where she observed that those who hadn't lost their homes experienced a profound "grief of adjacent loss" while survivors remained in shock. She shares her realization that accepting help from others enables a reciprocal flow of compassion, noting that this insight about the interconnected nature of giving and receiving assistance was something her parents and grandparents never fully embraced.
instruction.paragraph: Shortly after the fires, I gathered with a group of friends and neighbors near Altadena. Several had lost their houses, and many more had been evacuated with no idea when they’d be able to go home. The air was still heavy with smoke and the National Guard had set up blockades of the devastated streets, which were now lined with lot after lot of ash and rubble, almost nothing standing but chimneys and the occasional charred appliance.There were plenty of tears to go around, but I was struck by how those who hadn’t been directly affected were in some ways more capsized. Several admitted to survivor’s guilt. Even more expressed what I can only describe as the grief of adjacent loss.This grief, at least for the moment, seemed almost deeper in a way, more existential. While we who lost our homes were still cushioned by the shock of it all, others were left staring into a different kind of abyss. Without the granular distractions of insurance claims and cobbling together basic necessities, they were able — forced, actually — to take a step back and survey the full catastrophe. In their despair, their best source of comfort was to reach out a hand.“Please, please let us help,” one neighbor said, crying. “You must understand that we are asking this of you. This is for us as much as it is for you. Do not push us away.”I will undoubtedly learn countless lessons from this disaster, many of them bitter and unwanted. (For instance, the way GoFundMe can be a vehicle for the rich getting richer, since affluent people tend to have the most generous friends.) But the greatest so far has been the realization that help plays by the same rules as love.In order to give it, you must be willing to accept it. In accepting it, you open the valve for even more. I wish my parents and grandparents had been able to learn this lesson. Their lives would probably have been better for it.

first_draft.candidate: After the fires near Altadena, a gathering of friends and neighbors was organized, and I found myself reflecting on a sentiment I hadn't fully grasped before: the "grief of adjacent loss." Those of us who were fortunate enough to still have our homes felt an emptiness, a shadow cast over our relief by the sheer magnitude of loss surrounding us. Meanwhile, the survivors seemed suspended in disbelief, their eyes telling stories of recent horrors. As I moved through the crowd, conversations of support and gratitude filled the air, a collective healing of sorts. It hit me then—accepting help was more than just taking; it was opening a door to a cycle of compassion that allowed everyone to heal together. My parents and grandparents had always been strong in their resolve to give without taking, a trait born from another era's rugged sense of self-reliance. But in that moment, I felt the interconnectedness of giving and receiving, something they'd never truly embraced. It wasn't just about charity; it was about the strength found in community, in the merging of strangers' kindness with personal vulnerability. The shared experience that night taught me that offering help doesn't diminish the giver, nor does accepting help diminish the receiver. Instead, it forms a bridge, a tangible reminder that life's burdens are lighter when shared. I watched people exchange small smiles and words of encouragement as if reassuring each other that it was okay to lean on someone else just a little. The next step, I realized, was mine to take—to incorporate this revelation into my life, to teach it to my own children, to break the cycle of isolated stoicism. The gathering dwindled as dusk set in, but I lingered, absorbing the warmth from the people around me, holding onto the newly noticed truth that letting someone in doesn't only open you to help, but it also invites deeper connections into your life.

instruction.plot: The narrator, suffering from severe dizziness and vomiting while caring for their infant son, calls their friend Joy who immediately comes to help care for the baby while the narrator rests. After returning from Texas, the narrator grieves the loss of relationship with their parents but finds comfort in true friendships with people like Joy and Stacey, who demonstrate unconditional support during difficult times.
instruction.paragraph: One morning, I woke up dizzy and spent 20 minutes throwing up in the bathroom. I lay down on the linoleum floor while my son wiggled in his bouncy seat. I stared at his toes in tiny striped socks.When he needed a bottle, I wobbled downstairs, gripping the railing with one hand, and fed him while resting my head against the couch. Every time I moved, my brain felt like it was rattling. As soon as I sat down, I had to run back upstairs, buckle my son into his bouncy seat, and vomit again.I couldn’t do this. I called Joy.“I’m on the bathroom floor,” I said. “I can’t move.”I was so dizzy, I was afraid to carry him. I counted the time — two hours — until he would need another bottle, plotting how I’d make it downstairs.“I’ll be right there,” she said, and hung up.Ten minutes later, I heard the scrape of the front door open and close, water running in the kitchen while she washed her hands. She put on a face mask and, shaky, I walked downstairs with him. She sat with him on the couch while I napped in bed. When I emerged hours later, Joy was on the couch, and he was asleep in her arms. I no longer felt like I’d fall over.We were lucky. My son never got sick. And I began to know that we weren’t alone.After we returned from Texas, my mother sent infrequent, brief texts. She never apologized. I never heard from my father. The snow banks grew so high they had to be removed with dump trucks. I grieved the loss of my family.But in losing them, I also lost the constant messages that I wasn’t good enough, did not deserve their gifts, was bound for failure.Stacey, one of two friends who came to see us in Texas, drove from Michigan to sit with me in the neonatal intensive care unit for three days.“Love is not a tally sheet,” she told me. “I’m here because I want to be.”

first_draft.candidate: The room spun around me as I clutched the edge of the kitchen counter, trying to steady myself. Waves of nausea crashed over me, and I could barely keep my eyes open. My son, oblivious to my inner turmoil, lay in his crib, gurgling softly. I knew I couldn't take care of him like this. Through sheer force of will, I managed to reach my phone and call Joy. I didn't need to explain; she knew the tone in my voice was serious enough to drop everything. Before I knew it, she was at my door, her smile a balm on my rattled nerves. With her gentle assurance, I shuffled to bed, grateful for the chance to close my eyes. As I drifted in and out of a fevered sleep, I thought about my recent trip to Texas. Returning from there felt like stepping into a void. My relationship with my parents had frayed beyond recognition, and I left with an ache that no medicine could touch. Yet here, in my small world, people like Joy and Stacey filled those hollows with their kindness. They showed up when it mattered, no questions asked, no expectations in return. As I lay there, I realized that sometimes family isn't about blood but rather the people who stand by you when the ground feels unsteady. It was a solace to know I wasn't alone in this fragile dance of early motherhood, and it taught me that even amidst the loss, there were gains to cherish. instruction.plot: The paragraph argues that young men are facing educational, emotional, and cultural regression, with lower college graduation rates and increased retreat into video games, pornography, and "manosphere" figures like Andrew Tate and Joe Rogan, which may have influenced voting patterns in the 2024 presidential election where Donald Trump gained significant support from young men across racial groups. The author contends that literature, particularly novels, can help improve emotional intelligence and form identities, advocating for a more inclusive literary culture that encourages young men to read and write without diminishing progress for women writers.
instruction.paragraph: In recent decades, young men have regressed educationally, emotionally and culturally. Among women matriculating at four-year public colleges, about half will graduate four years later; for men the rate is under 40 percent. This disparity surely translates to a drop-off in the number of novels young men read, as they descend deeper into video games and pornography. Young men who still exhibit curiosity about the world too often seek intellectual stimulation through figures of the “manosphere” such as Andrew Tate and Joe Rogan.The marginalization of young men seems to have been a significant factor in this year’s presidential election. No voters were more committed to Mr. Trump than young white men — and he also did well with Hispanic men and continued to make gains with Black men. I think of 2024 as the “Fight Club” election, in which disaffected guys vented their frustrations and anxieties through a brawler who will one day reveal himself to be not their hero, but rather a figment of their imagination.These young men need better stories — and they need to see themselves as belonging to the world of storytelling. Novels do many things. They entertain, inspire, puzzle, hypnotize. But reading fiction is also an excellent way to improve one’s emotional I.Q. Novels help us form our identities and understand our lives. Like many other bookish Gen X-ers, I can’t conceive of my formative years without the Douglas Coupland novel that gave our generation its name. This is why we need a more inclusive literary culture, one that will bring young men in from the cold.I am not saying that we should declare progress for women writers complete and now focus only on men. The question for me is: What will become of literature — and indeed, of society — if men are no longer involved in reading and writing? The fortunes of men and women are intertwined. This is why, for example, I make sure that my male students read “The Handmaid’s Tale.” It’s not just their edification that matters; women also benefit from the existence of better men.

first_draft.candidate: As I look around at my peers, I see a troubling trend that can't be ignored. Many of us young men seem to be retreating into worlds that offer easy escapes but little growth: endless video games, the detachment of online adult content, and the unquestioning reverence for figures like Andrew Tate and Joe Rogan. It's as if we're collectively stepping back from reaching our potential, with fewer of us finishing college and more of us getting caught up in the echo chambers of the "manosphere." This shift could be seen in the last presidential election, where Donald Trump surprisingly garnered strong support from young men across different racial backgrounds. It made me wonder: what are we missing in our emotional and cultural diets? I believe immersing ourselves in literature could be a way forward. Novels offer perspectives that challenge and enrich our emotional intelligence, helping us understand and articulate our identities better. It's not about abandoning manhood but expanding it in ways that are thoughtful and empathetic. Cultivating a culture that encourages young men to both read and write can foster a more nuanced understanding of the world without taking away from the progress that's been made by women writers. Instead of rejecting these powerful narratives, we should incorporate them, enriching our understanding of what it means to be in today's world. Encouraging this literary engagement doesn't mean leaving behind the parts of our culture that are compelling to us but rather finding a balance that adds depth and meaning. So, as we confront the challenges unique to our generation, I hope we can broaden our horizons, allowing the stories we engage with to shape and refine us, guiding us to be not just competent but compassionate participants in the world.

instruction.plot: The paragraph describes liberal academic introspection following a presidential election defeat, suggesting that Democrats have become disconnected from working-class Americans despite having beneficial policies. It cites several factors for the loss—inflation, wage gaps, low presidential approval ratings—while arguing that Donald Trump successfully exploited social divisions to win, demonstrating that unity-focused campaigns struggle in a deeply polarized society.
instruction.paragraph: The worst thing we university liberals could do right now is to keep wondering why “they” hate us, why blue-collar workers seem to vote — as we understand it — against their own interests in sidling up to an authoritarian in a red tie who courts other billionaires, or why human nature itself did not come through for us and make the arc of history bend toward justice as we define it.History has been waiting to explode our hubris; and sometimes, even as we have facts, truth and rule of law on our side, we make ourselves good targets with our jargon, our righteousness and our fragmentation. We are out of touch with working class Americans, even if the policies that Democrats have enacted work for them.There were signs a Democratic defeat was coming: high inflation; a stubborn wage gap, especially between women with and without a college degree; and the incumbent president’s low approval ratings. A brilliant Black woman opponent ran an honorable campaign about unity in a fractured political culture riddled with fierce tribalism. Donald Trump exploited our social fissures to make them deeper, uglier, ever more bitter and therefore useful. We were reminded that culture wars are won by fueling them, not by seeking harmony. Unity coalitions and kindness and joy don’t win elections in a bitterly divided society where neighbors and family members are not on the same team.

first_draft.candidate: In the aftermath of our electoral defeat, we find ourselves grappling with the uncomfortable reality that our connection with working-class Americans has waned. Despite policies we believe could genuinely improve lives, there's a sense they're not resonating as they should. The specter of inflation and wage gaps loomed large in the minds of voters, compounded by unflattering presidential approval ratings that seemed to overshadow the benefits we touted. Meanwhile, Donald Trump's ability to harness and amplify social divisions became apparent, leaving us to reflect on whether our focus on unity is enough in a landscape marked by polarization. We came together with visions of bridging divides, yet his success lays bare a discomforting truth—perhaps forging consensus is trickier than acknowledging the chasms. It's a moment that calls for introspection, urging us to consider how to better articulate our aims to those who feel we've lost touch with their everyday struggles. As we sift through the myriad factors contributing to our collective setback, there's an underlying recognition that strategies valuing connection and understanding must evolve. Looking ahead, we face the challenge of reimagining our approach in a way that resonates more deeply. This isn't merely about recalibration but about genuinely listening and responding to the voices that felt unheard in the cacophony of campaign promises.

instruction.plot: The author reflects on how students may lack motivation to engage in academic effort due to a perception that success depends more on luck and connections than knowledge, yet finds hope in those who show genuine intellectual curiosity. Despite universities emphasizing earning potential and embracing influencer culture, the author remains committed to demonstrating the value of thoughtful reading, discussion, and revision while allowing students to make their own choices about resisting intellectual inertia.
instruction.paragraph: All in all, it looks as if success follows not from knowledge and skill but from luck, hype and access to the right companies. If this is the economy students believe they’re entering, then why should they make the effort to read? For that matter, how will any effort in school prepare them for careers in which, apparently, effort is not rewarded?Given all this, it’s easy to lose faith in humanistic learning. Universities themselves offer little solace. They constantly promote the idea that a degree is about earning power above all else. They embrace influencer culture and probably benefit from viral phenomena like Bama Rush. They certainly aren’t shooing away corporate recruiters.But teaching is an inherently hopeful profession, and as much as students worry me, they also give me hope. I often see my writing students push themselves past what’s easy or rational. They get excited about their research projects; sometimes they even ponder whether to use a period or a semicolon to separate two sentences.The fact is, not all students aim to sail on vibes. Some want to do work that makes more than money. Some finance majors do, too. And others, God bless them, just want to learn what they can and worry about work later.It’s up to students to decide whether they’ll resist intellectual inertia. All I can do is demonstrate that it is worth it to read, to pause, to think, to revise, to reread, to discuss, to revise again. I can, in the time students are with me, offer them chances to defy their incentives and see what happens.

first_draft.candidate: As I stand before my students, I often sense a quiet skepticism in the room. Many of them seem unconvinced that hard work and knowledge will pave a path to success. They whisper about the importance of connections or about the role of sheer luck, rather than discussing the merits of their own intellect and dedication. Yet, every so often, I encounter a student who surprises me. These students aren't driven by the promises of high earning potential or the allure of online fame. Instead, they question deeply, read with genuine interest, and engage in discussions that ignite their curiosity. It's these brief encounters that keep my hope alive. Universities today seem fixated on marketable skills and a culture that values quick fame over profound understanding. Even so, I remain steadfast in my belief that thoughtful reading, meaningful discussion, and the process of revision are undeniably valuable. I can't force this perspective on my students; they must arrive at it in their own time, if at all. Though some may eventually buy into the superficial allure of influencers, others might quietly resist, finding their way back to intellectual pursuits that truly matter to them. I watch and wait, eager to support their journeys regardless of the direction they choose. It's about planting seeds, knowing that not every seed will take root immediately, if at all. My role isn't to dictate a path, but to present the options and encourage contemplation. Hope, after all, is a patient visitor in the classroom.

instruction.plot: The writer describes how Facebook's chaotic, camp-value appeal offers an escape from the constraining algorithms of other platforms, comparing it to cult films and bad chain restaurants while appreciating its bizarre charm. They enjoy lurking in diverse Facebook groups as a voyeur, consuming content not targeted at them specifically, which provides a refreshing "bazaar" experience unlike other social media where algorithms narrowly define and target user interests.
instruction.paragraph: The reason I love Facebook is the same reason I believe “Spice World” should be added to the Criterion Collection — I find its camp value to be thrilling and irresistible. Facebook is a veritable freak show, and its appeal rests on the same “so bad it’s good” logic that informs my love of ’70s cult film and objectively terrible chain restaurants. But it’s also more than that. By joining myriad disparate groups, I’ve managed to turn a dinosaur platform into a refreshing escape hatch from the algorithm that rules over our collective digital lives.The “algorithm” is a stifling and mysterious boogeyman that controls every aspect of modernity, from the people you match with on dating apps to the route by which you drive home from work. Of course the algorithm is not one thing but many: a series of mathematical calculations that lack sentience but in their sheer ubiquity compose what can feel like an omniscient digital overlord.When I listen to music, it’s whatever the Spotify algorithm has determined sounds like Pavement instead of the vast library of beloved songs I collected on iTunes. When I visit Instagram, I am served reels of unqualified people giving questionable dating advice thanks to a recent breakup as opposed to welcome updates from friends and family. TikTok is dead set on its insistence I am bisexual, nonbinary and have a mental illness — and I’m starting to think it’s right.But on Facebook, I am completely free of the assumptions these other apps have formed about me.I lurk in the shadows, like the creepiest of voyeurs, reading passionate discussions of the flipping of meme stocks and harrowing tales of marital woe aimed toward fellow moms, or absorbing photos of sumptuous feasts prepared by outdoor cooking enthusiasts.Facebook has become my modern-day version of a bazaar, with its rows of tiny stalls offering untold treasures. None of it was meant for me, and yet I appreciate it all, taking it in with the beauty and appreciation of a collector.

first_draft.candidate: Scrolling through Facebook feels like sifting through a digital flea market, each corner offering some unexpected trinket or oddity. There's a certain allure in its haphazard mix of content, reminiscent of low-budget cult films or that quirky comfort one finds in a subpar chain restaurant with eccentric decor. It's fascinating to dive into this chaotic theater where the usual algorithmic restraints that bind us on other platforms momentarily loosen. Unlike Instagram's unyielding push of tailored aesthetics or Twitter's echo chambers, Facebook stands out with its charmingly unpredictable landscape. Here, I find myself lurking in groups themed around hobbies I have no intention of pursuing—like mid-century modern furniture or extreme couponing—just for the sheer novelty of it. These spaces haven't been perfectly curated for me, and that's exactly why I enjoy them. It's refreshing to escape from the narrow corridors of hyper-targeted content, experiencing a sort of voyeuristic joy witnessing passions I don't share. Facebook, in its peculiar charm, offers a genuine bazaar feel, an unfiltered mesh of humanity in all its glorious oddities and banalities. Unlike other platforms, where every click is analyzed and spit back at me in neatly digestible, ultra-specific bites, Facebook's offerings can be aimless and beautifully inefficient. It has this uncanny ability to dish out the unexpectedly absurd alongside the sincere and poignant, all in one scroll. Somehow, the curated chaos serves as an escape, a respite where I'm not constantly boxed into a neat algorithmic identity. Perhaps that's what makes Facebook strangely liberating, despite its often clunky facade. It remains a unique, albeit messy, sanctuary where the thrill is not in finding exactly what I want but in stumbling upon what I never knew I needed.

instruction.plot: The author was drawn to Puerto Vallarta after watching "The Night of the Iguana" on TV, becoming captivated by the lush Mexican landscape rather than the overheated plot or acting. Though once a Hollywood hotspot in the 1960s and 70s that later experienced a tourism boom, Puerto Vallarta has since been overshadowed by other Mexican destinations like Cancún and Cabo San Lucas, yet the author was attracted to its perceived authenticity compared to these more "cocoon-like" resort towns.
instruction.paragraph: I first traveled to the Mexican resort town of Puerto Vallarta because of a decades-old, black-and-white movie. On a frigid winter night, as I was flipping channels in my Manhattan apartment, I stumbled across a showing of “The Night of the Iguana” on Turner Classic Movies.This 1964 adaptation of the Tennessee Williams play, directed by John Huston and starring Richard Burton and Ava Gardner, was not exactly a film classic. The story was overheated; the acting even more so. But as it played out on my TV screen, I began paying less attention to the plot and more to the lush landscape on which it played out.The coastal town, set in the Mexican state of Jalisco, and cradled by the gorgeous Bahía de Banderas to the west and the sweeping Sierra Madre mountain range to the east, was briefly a tourist hot spot in the 1960s and early ’70s, helped in part by the Hollywood crowd that flocked there after Huston, et al., came back and raved about it to their friends. Later, an international airport made it more accessible, and tourism boomed.Over the years, though, Puerto Vallarta was eclipsed by Cancún, Cabo San Lucas, Tulum and even Sayulita, a surfing destination just a few miles up the Pacific Coast. Though undeniably beautiful, with access to fantastic beaches, those places felt to me blandly familiar — sprawling resorts that, for the most part, seemed to be offering a cocoon-like escape from the actual country of Mexico. I wanted something a little less predictable and, for lack of a better term, a little more “authentic.”

first_draft.candidate: After watching "The Night of the Iguana," my fascination with Puerto Vallarta took root, not so much because of the film's tempestuous drama or the overblown performances, but rather the verdant, unfettered beauty of the Mexican landscape it showcased. I could almost feel the humid air on my skin as the screen flickered with images of rugged cliffs and vibrant greenery. Puerto Vallarta spoke to me, whispering of a time when it held a certain unspoiled charm before it became a darling of Hollywood stars back in the 1960s and 70s and even pre-tourism boom. Nowadays, its luster might be considered somewhat dimmed by the emergence of Cancún and Cabo San Lucas as the jewels of Mexican tourism. Yet, that's precisely why I find myself drawn to it even more. There's an authenticity that Puerto Vallarta has maintained, perhaps due to being overshadowed by the polished, resort-driven hype that envelops these newer tourist havens. The other destinations, with their all-inclusive packages, offer a sort of escape that feels almost too convenient, like living in a bubble of tailored experiences. Puerto Vallarta, on the other hand, beckons with the promise of something real, an encounter with Mexico that's not entirely curated. Here, I'd imagine, one might find a rhythm of life that allows for slowing down, feeling the pulse of the place itself rather than just passing through. In this way, Puerto Vallarta holds an allure of a different kind, a sense of place that's more discovery than destination.
