instruction.plot: The author, initially disliking New York City after moving there for graduate school in 2016, began collecting obscure facts about locations throughout the city as a way to make sense of their new environment and eventually obtained a tour guide license. By 2023, they overcame their hesitation and began leading free walking tours with a friend, using equipment like clipboards and speakers to share their accumulated knowledge about the city's history, architecture, and cultural landmarks with both organized groups and informal gatherings.
instruction.paragraph: A friend introduced the idea to me back in 2016. I had just moved to New York for graduate school, and I hated the city: It was too loud, I was always lost and everything reeked. But I was an active Wikipedia user, and began accumulating mostly useless facts in the hope that they’d make the city make sense. Walking down Wooster Street, I would stop and tell my companions to look up. “On the second floor of this building, there’s a room with nothing but 280,000 pounds of dirt in it,” I’d tell them. “It’s called ‘The New York Earth Room,’ by the artist Walter De Maria.” Passing by the famous Flatiron Building on 23rd Street, I’d allow out-of-town visitors a moment of silent appreciation before pulling them across Fifth Avenue. “This is not just any Starbucks,” I’d say. “This is the house where the novelist Edith Wharton grew up.” In isolation, each detail amounted to little more than a point in bar trivia. Individually, those facts felt meaningless; together, though, they made me feel at home in the city. I imagined that leading a real tour would give form and function to all the information rattling around inside my head.Even after I earned my license, I struggled to make the leap from fact hoarder to talking-while-walking-backward guide. Did other people even care about this stuff? And if they did, who would want to listen to me opine? In the spring of 2023, a friend finally persuaded me to put our licenses to use and start leading free walking tours across the city. We purchased clipboards, horse-training flags to wave as we walked and — after a few complaints that traffic drowned us out — cheap speakers to hang around our necks and project our voices. Through the nonprofit Municipal Art Society of New York, we’ve organized some walks that emphasize how we see the city’s history and politics expressed in its built environment. Others are for friends, family and whoever else might find us on Instagram, presumably via their own niche interests.

first_draft.candidate: When I first moved to New York City for grad school in 2016, the place felt overwhelmingly chaotic and impersonal. To cope, I started collecting obscure facts about various corners of the city—tiny details that made the vastness seem a little more manageable. For instance, I learned about the intricacies of the Brooklyn Bridge's construction mishaps and where you can still see remnants of horse-drawn trolley tracks peeking through asphalt in Manhattan. What began as a strange hobby gradually became a driving curiosity, and before I knew it, I'd gathered enough facts to fill a notebook. Deciding to formalize my knowledge, I took the plunge and obtained a tour guide license, never really expecting to use it. Yet, by 2023, a friend and I decided to step out of our comfort zones and start leading walking tours, offering them for free as a way to lure people into our world of trivia and history. Armed with clipboards and portable speakers, we'd venture out with groups—sometimes organized, other times just a bunch of curious locals and tourists we'd managed to gather spontaneously. Our stops included the usual hotspots but also lesser-known gems: an unassuming building that once housed a groundbreaking artists' collective or a forgotten cemetery hidden behind tall skyscrapers. Slowly, I found myself embracing the city, its quirks, and its contrasts, feeling that these tours were as much about rediscovering New York as they were about sharing it with others. Translating the files I'd gathered in my head into stories and anecdotes enriched my relationship with the city, turning what was once an alienating metropolis into a vibrant tapestry of history and culture. Even my initial hesitation transformed into enthusiasm as I interacted with strangers who shared their own snippets of knowledge, forever changing the landscape of my understanding. Offering these tours might have started as an experiment, but they've become a bridge, connecting not just the city to its past but me to my newfound home.

instruction.plot: A journalist recalls a late-night adventure in Tokyo's gay district where they danced with a Japanese salaryman at a hidden disco, while their husband (who doesn't normally smoke) smoked and chatted about music with a DJ friend named Ken. The experience represents how they transform into different people while in Tokyo, contrasting with their ordinary life in New York and evoking memories of when the journalist lived in Japan as a foreign correspondent years ago.
instruction.paragraph: By 3 a.m., I was dancing to “Material Girl” with a Japanese man in a plaid vest. We were on the crowded dance floor of a disco on the second floor of a nondescript office building tucked at the end of a little alley in Shinjuku Ni-chome, Tokyo’s gay district.Using my broken Japanese, I learned that my dance partner was a salaryman by day, slaving away at one of those soul-sucking Japanese office jobs. But this night, he was singing along to Madonna at the New Sazae bar, vamping it up as if we were in an episode of “Club MTV.”He wasn’t the only one pretending. On most nights at home in New York, my husband, Robert, and I are in bed by 10:30 p.m. The only dancing I do takes place clumsily in an overpriced indoor cycling class. Living it up means a second glass of wine at dinner.But here, in the wee hours, Robert stood in a corner, smoking. (He is not a smoker.) He and Ken Nishikawa, a D.J. friend who speaks English with a British accent and some­times goes by the stage name Intelligent Milli Vanilli (which is a phonetic challenge for the Japanese), were engaged in a deep conversation about the Pet Shop Boys. Ken’s wife, Ayumi, drunk on sake, practiced her aikido moves on a woman (I think) in frosted lipstick and teased hair.This is who we are in Tokyo, where it seems nothing is as it should be back home, even if we want it to be.My trip all seems like a dream now, but then so does my old life, when I lived there as a foreign correspondent for The Wall Street Journal and Robert and I were dating long distance. Neither of us had been to Japan since I moved back to the United States in late 2007.My plan was to revisit all of my favorite places, starting with recreating my very first night in Tokyo nearly a decade ago, when Ken, a friend of a friend who was eager to show a gaijin (foreigner) around, first took me through a portal to a world that I never would have discovered on my own.

first_draft.candidate: The neon lights flickered in vibrant hues as I slipped into a tucked-away disco in Tokyo's lively gay district, my senses already buzzing with familiar anticipation. Entering the compact, dimly lit space was like stepping into a parallel existence—Tokyo always had a way of doing that to me. Across the room, my husband stood relaxed, a cigarette between his fingers, laughing with our DJ friend Ken, something he'd never do back home in New York. There's something about Tokyo that unfurls hidden facets in us both, encouraged perhaps by these late-night adventures in a city that once served as my beat as a foreign correspondent. It often feels like the city remembers me too, offering a canvas to paint a different version of myself each time I return. I found myself drawn into the kinetic rhythm of the disco, where a Japanese salaryman, his shirt clinging to him under the pulsing lights, broke away from the edge of the dance floor. We caught each other's eye and began moving together, our awkward initial steps giving way to something more fluid as the crowd surged around us. His laughter was infectious, a bright contrast against the relentless pace of his workaday life. In that moment, we were free, buoyed by the music and the gentle anonymity the city afforded us. It felt like I was back in my reporting days when every corner turned promised a new story, every stranger a new world. Watching my husband and Ken animatedly discuss old records and club scenes took me back to endless nights when dense clouds of cigarette smoke swirled in tiny music bars during my Tokyo years, a comforting mix of nostalgia and novelty. By the time we left, the city was quieter, but it thrummed with the same vibrant energy I had first fallen in love with. Walking hand in hand through winding streets, I wondered how Tokyo held this ability—the power to transform us into versions of ourselves we rarely see but have somehow always been there, waiting to emerge under the city's ever-watchful, neon glow.

instruction.plot: A woman with a longtime fascination for péniches (French riverboats) meets a Dutch couple in Paris who invites her aboard their boat for drinks, where she experiences the peaceful charm of sleeping on water while enjoying spectacular views of the city. After thirty years of admiring these vessels from afar, she expresses interest in possibly renting one for a future stay, foreshadowing her eventual June experience when she fulfills this dream of staying on a boat docked in Paris.
instruction.paragraph: There’s something about sleeping on a boat. It’s the rocking, of course, and the sound of the water. It’s also the cocoon effect of containment in a small space tucked away from the world. I’m not talking about cruise ships and luxury yachts here. I’m talking about a vessel that gently rocks, just enough to let a person know she’s not on dry land. If you suffer from seasickness, this could be an issue. As for me, I never sleep better than I do on a boat.Now imagine this boat is docked in Paris. You wake up to a view straight out of a French movie from the 1950s and finish your day under a full moon.In June I got to experience that (all but the full moon, but more on that later).My fixation was not a recent one. I’d been eyeing boats — specifically péniches, riverboats used originally for commercial purposes — for more than 30 years, as long as I’d been visiting Paris. Then, at a party in Paris last fall, my last night in the city before heading home to the United States, I met a Dutch couple — Jan and Lydia — who invited me to their péniche for a drink.Docked along the Right Bank — midway between the Pont de la Concorde and the Passerelle Léopold-Sédar-Senghor — my new friends’ péniche sat in the middle of my favorite city, but in a world of its own, away from traffic and crowds. As perfect a combination as I could dream up.The evening was warm. We sat on the deck as Jan set out wine glasses and a bottle of Champagne. Across the water, the Eiffel Tower sparkled.“If you ever hear of someone who might like to rent their péniche for a week or two,” I said, “let me know.”

first_draft.candidate: For years, my interest in peniches had been like a quiet current running parallel to the river's edge. I would spend afternoons strolling the Seine, imagining what it might be like on board one of those peaceful floating homes. My fascination remained a daydream until one evening in Paris, when chance and a warm smile brought the fantasy closer. I met a Dutch couple, friendly and unassuming, who owned a peniche moored gracefully along the city's banks. They invited me aboard for drinks, and stepping onto their boat felt like crossing into a different world. Comfortably seated with a glass in hand, I took in the gentle bobbing beneath my feet, the Seine's quiet whispers, and the city skyline glowing softly as daylight thinned into night. We talked about the subtle joys of life on water, the way the world seemed a little kinder from their vantage point. When I mentioned my longstanding dream of renting a peniche, their encouraging words were the nudge I needed. As we toasted to new friendships, I found myself contemplating the possibility more seriously than before. The seed of an idea slowly took root, reminding me with quiet assurance that one day, June would come, and with it, the realization of living along the Seine, even if just for a while. The thought lingered pleasantly as we said our goodbyes, and I stepped back onto solid ground, carrying with me the serene images from the boat that drifted into my dreams, gently urging me toward what was now not just a wistful desire but a burgeoning plan. From that evening, my walks by the river turned into moments of eager anticipation, knowing that soon, I would be one of those living in the quiet embrace of a peniche in Paris.

instruction.plot: A social media user celebrates Facebook as a delightful escape from algorithmic control, comparing it to cult films and "so bad it's good" entertainment like "Spice World." By joining diverse groups, they enjoy voyeuristically exploring communities discussing everything from meme stocks to cooking, experiencing the platform as a modern-day bazaar of untold treasures free from the targeted assumptions that dominate other social media platforms.
instruction.paragraph: The reason I love Facebook is the same reason I believe “Spice World” should be added to the Criterion Collection — I find its camp value to be thrilling and irresistible. Facebook is a veritable freak show, and its appeal rests on the same “so bad it’s good” logic that informs my love of ’70s cult film and objectively terrible chain restaurants. But it’s also more than that. By joining myriad disparate groups, I’ve managed to turn a dinosaur platform into a refreshing escape hatch from the algorithm that rules over our collective digital lives.The “algorithm” is a stifling and mysterious boogeyman that controls every aspect of modernity, from the people you match with on dating apps to the route by which you drive home from work. Of course the algorithm is not one thing but many: a series of mathematical calculations that lack sentience but in their sheer ubiquity compose what can feel like an omniscient digital overlord.When I listen to music, it’s whatever the Spotify algorithm has determined sounds like Pavement instead of the vast library of beloved songs I collected on iTunes. When I visit Instagram, I am served reels of unqualified people giving questionable dating advice thanks to a recent breakup as opposed to welcome updates from friends and family. TikTok is dead set on its insistence I am bisexual, nonbinary and have a mental illness — and I’m starting to think it’s right.But on Facebook, I am completely free of the assumptions these other apps have formed about me.I lurk in the shadows, like the creepiest of voyeurs, reading passionate discussions of the flipping of meme stocks and harrowing tales of marital woe aimed toward fellow moms, or absorbing photos of sumptuous feasts prepared by outdoor cooking enthusiasts.Facebook has become my modern-day version of a bazaar, with its rows of tiny stalls offering untold treasures. None of it was meant for me, and yet I appreciate it all, taking it in with the beauty and appreciation of a collector.

first_draft.candidate:
I've found myself delightfully lost on Facebook, and it feels oddly refreshing. Unlike the polished chaos of other social media apps, Facebook has turned into a quirky escape, sort of like watching a cult classic film or revisiting "Spice World" in all its messy glory. It's the kind of journey where you appreciate the jagged edges rather than seamless narratives. I join groups with eclectic interests, drawn into worlds I never knew existed. One minute, I'm piecing together theories on meme stocks and the next, I'm delving into debates over the perfect sourdough starter. It's voyeuristic, sure, but in a way that feels genuinely explorative rather than invasive.

On Facebook, each group is like a bustling stall in a sprawling bazaar. Sure, there's clutter and chaos, but that's part of the charm. I lose track of time clicking through discussions I never intended to find but somehow can't stop reading. What fascinates me is the unpredictable mix of voices and perspectives, free from the algorithmic precision stalking me elsewhere online. On those other platforms, there's this sense that everything I might want or care about is pre-decided, neatly packaged, and presented with eerie precision. In contrast, Facebook offers a kind of freedom from that algorithmic gaze, where I stumble upon the unexpected like a treasure hunter, discovering communities and conversations that are delightfully offbeat.

These digital interactions, this motley stew of content, feel less about profit and more about people. There's a delight in the randomness, an excitement in finding joy in the uncurated. When I scroll through these groups, there's a sense that I'm peeking through countless windows into the vibrant houses of other people's lives. It's the digital equivalent of wandering through a market, every corner promising a new sight, smell, or sound. Sure, it's a little chaotic, with the air thick with the chatter of voices competing for attention, but that's precisely what makes it enchanting.

instruction.plot: In Marseille, France's vibrant port city, late-night culture centers around pizza with distinctive local characteristics—featuring harder crusts, Emmental cheese instead of mozzarella, and Provençal marjoram instead of oregano. The diverse pizza varieties, from the moitié-moitié to Armenian and Corsican styles, serve as a culinary representation of the city's multicultural heritage shaped by successive waves of immigration from Italy, Armenia, Corsica, and North Africa.
instruction.paragraph: On a balmy night in Marseille, France’s second-largest city, crowds move through the graffiti-toned streets of the central Cours Julien neighborhood. Buildings are splashed in color as if the nearby Mediterranean had washed up, ebbed out and left behind pigments of a shattered rainbow.It’s almost midnight. The square is still buzzing with people cracking jokes and taking swigs of pastis. Restaurants are mostly closed, but a warm glow beckons from open counters, where the scent of tomato sauce, cheese and dough wafts through the air.“Here, the late-night food isn’t really kebabs or crepes,” my Marseille-native friend Simon told me when I moved to the city just over a year ago. “It’s pizza.”Marseille pizza has a harder crust than the soft Neapolitan style. It’s typically made with Emmental cheese instead of mozzarella. Some say this is simply because Emmental was traditionally more readily available; others swear it’s saltier and richer. Pizza makers frequently swap Provençal marjoram for oregano; sometimes they sprinkle raw garlic on top.The classic Marseille slice is the moitié-moitié (half-half), a tomato-based pie with anchovies on one side and cheese on the other. The Armenian has minced beef, onions and peppers. Sweet figatelli sausage and brousse cheese, which is similar to ricotta, top the Corsican slice. Halal pizza is available in Noailles, a neighborhood near the port.That variety reflects the city itself. Italians first brought pizza to Marseille in the late 19th century, and since then, waves of immigrants, from places like Armenia, Corsica, and Algeria, have all embraced the dish and made it their own.“It’s not very different from other big industrial port cities, but the difference in Marseille, a bit like New York maybe, is that there’s a sort of narrative of cosmopolitanism,” Céline Regnard, a local historian, said. “The city thinks of itself as a melting pot.”Marseille is a mosaic of the people, culture and history that shape it. Pizza is a way to explore that mosaic.

first_draft.candidate: Strolling through Marseille's lively streets at night, I'm always drawn to the aroma of pizza wafting through the warm air. Here, the pizzas are unlike any I've had elsewhere, distinctly crafted with local flair and a nod to the city's multicultural roots. The crusts are a bit harder than usual, offering a satisfying crunch with each bite, and the cheese of choice is Emmental, giving each slice a slightly nutty tang. Instead of the familiar oregano, a sprinkle of Provençal marjoram adds a unique herbal touch, grounding the flavors in a sense of place. The variety is staggering, reflecting a blending of cultures that defines Marseille. I might start with a moitié-moitié, a harmonious blend of flavors that doesn't adhere to strict culinary rules, much like the city itself. Then there are the Armenian styles, often topped with spicy sausage, a nod to the Armenian families who have settled here over the years. The Corsican varieties, rich with the island's traditional charcuterie, also speak to another layer of Marseille's heritage. This city-by-the-sea tells its story through food, each pizza offering a slice of history shaped by those who have come and added their influences over generations. It's fascinating to think that something as simple as pizza could carry such depth and narrative. As I savor each slice, I find myself connected not just to the local ingredients but to the history and people who have shaped this place. In the midst of these bustling streets, under the starry sky, there's a sense of continuity and connection—a shared understanding that this is what makes Marseille so vibrant and alive. It's more than just a meal; it's an experience, an edible history lesson, and a reminder that food can be a powerful link to culture and community.

instruction.plot: The author visited Crete with their family, exploring ancient Minoan ruins at the Palace of Knossos with a tour guide who used augmented reality to show children how the palace once looked, while also revealing that many traditional historical narratives about King Minos and the Minotaur were inaccurate. During their stay near Chania, they enjoyed local cuisine, observed architectural influences from various historical conquerors, and hiked through gorges with Greek friends, culminating in a philosophical lesson from their guide about forgiving "the Minotaur within."
instruction.paragraph: After our Athens whirlwind, we flew to Crete, where the ancient Minoan civilization blossomed 5,000 years ago while the rest of Europe was mired in barbarianism.With our Greek friends, we hiked gorges and built intricate palaces on pink-sand beaches. We stayed outside the port city of Chania, where the signs of various conquerors are still in evidence, including Ottoman baths, Venetian arsenals and a graceful Egyptian lighthouse perched on the end of a long sea wall. We drank raki, the local liquor, and devoured seafood, like razor-thin sea bass carpaccio, and early harvest, locally made olive oil.At the Palace of Knossos, the seat of the Minoan Empire, we had another terrific tour guide, Akrivi Hatzigeorgiou, with the KidsLoveGreece.com tour company. She promptly handed all the children iPads with augmented reality apps that allowed them to see the ruins as they once were.Akrivi showed us the palace’s sophisticated water management systems, the hidden network of signage and the throne room, with one of the oldest preserved chairs in Europe. We did not see the Minotaur that, as any good Greek child historian knows, supposedly haunted the labyrinth in the basement. In fact, we learned there was no basement at all and that there never was a King Minos, but rather a series of female rulers, a detail which had been conveniently overlooked by historians and storytellers since. Hearing this, Holt’s brain exploded. History evolves.At the end of the tour, Akrivi thanked us. “The labyrinth is in our heads,” she said to the bewildered children. “The Minotaur is inside of us. We cannot beat the Minotaur, we must forgive the Minotaur.” Max nodded, as though he had known this all along.

first_draft.candidate: During our visit to Crete, my family and I explored the curious blend of history and modern technology at the Palace of Knossos. Our guide, equipped with augmented reality tools, transfixed our children by bringing the ancient ruins to life, showing them vivid reconstructions of what the palace once may have looked like. It was fascinating to watch them engage with history in such an interactive way. As we delved deeper, the guide dispelled some conventional myths about King Minos and the Minotaur, challenging what we traditionally believed and prompting us to rethink those ancient stories. Our stay near Chania was equally enriching. The local cuisine was a delightful array of tastes, seasoned by a history of varied conquerors leaving their culinary marks. As we explored the architecture, it became clear how layered the island's past is, with each occupying force leaving its own imprint. With Greek friends, we hiked through some of the island's stunning gorges, a physical journey that subtly mirrored the inner exploration the trip inspired. Our guide remarked on embracing and forgiving "the Minotaur within"—a metaphor that lingered with me long afterward, suggesting a need to reconcile with our own imperfections. Crete was more than a vacation; it was a poignant reminder of how history, personal and shared, often demands a nuanced understanding and acceptance.

instruction.plot: Prague is experiencing a renaissance beyond its historic center, with new boutiques, restaurants, and amenities appearing in previously overlooked neighborhoods like Smichov, Vinohrady, and Zizkov that are easily accessible via excellent public transportation. Following the pandemic's tourism reset, the city has become more resident-focused, with its best new cafes, bars, and restaurants emerging in areas outside Old Town such as Dejvice, Holesovice, Karlin, and New Town.
instruction.paragraph: Prague has become one of the most visited cities in Europe for good reason: remarkable architecture, rich history and excellent drinking and eating options. Once thought of as slightly behind the times, the Czech capital is also experiencing a renewed interest in design and fashion, with dozens of new shops. Happily, many of the best new boutiques, restaurants and pubs are either outside or on the edge of the heavily touristed city center. Thanks to Prague’s excellent public transportation, you can whiz from new attractions in the once-ignored neighborhood of Smichov, south of the guidebook sites in the Mala Strana district, out to the residential but party-friendly areas of Vinohrady and Zizkov east of Old Town. Even in more central areas, catching up on Prague’s cutting edge usually means avoiding crowds.A reset on tourism during the pandemic has left the city feeling more focused on local residents, with many new parks, bike trails, pedestrian bridges and other amenities showing up outside the historic center. The best new cafes, bars and restaurants, as well, are often found outside Old Town, in neighborhoods like Dejvice, Vinohrady, Holesovice, Karlin and New Town. Stop by for a coffee, hit up one of the many great new bakeries or visit a charismatic old beer hall as you explore a city that is clearly entering its prime.

first_draft.candidate:
In recent years, Prague has quietly embarked on a new chapter, one that extends beyond the ornate facades of its historic center. Neighborhoods like Smichov, Vinohrady, and Zizkov, once overshadowed by the grandeur of the Old Town, are now bustling with life and promise. These areas, easily reachable through the city's impressive public transportation network, have emerged as vibrant canvases for innovation and connection. The pandemic-induced halt in tourism forced a reevaluation of the city's cultural and economic landscape. As the bustling crowds thinned, Prague turned inward, focusing on its residents and reshaping itself into a city that caters as much to its local populace as to the globe-trotting visitors who often dominate its central streets.

This shift has led to the rise of lively new cafes, bars, and restaurants, sprouting up not in the expected heart of the city but in its more residential districts like Dejvice, Holesovice, Karlin, and New Town. Each of these neighborhoods has crafted its own identity, fostering local businesses that reflect a range of influences, from traditional Czech heritage to global culinary trends. The energy is palpable as each street corner might reveal a new boutique selling handcrafted goods or a modest eatery that plays with modern takes on classic dishes.

Residents find a newfound pride in their surroundings, a reclaiming of spaces that had been primarily oriented towards tourists. This evolution sees Prague seamlessly balancing its storied past with contemporary growth, offering a narrative where history and modernity coexist. As a result, locals and visitors alike are invited to explore beyond the traditional confines of cobbled pathways and Gothic archways, encouraged to discover the latent vibrancy in lesser-known areas. The transformation of these neighborhoods into thriving hubs illustrates a city in flux, one that acknowledges its roots while daring to redefine itself. In this way, Prague's renaissance skirts grandiosity; it embraces a subtler, more personal rejuvenation, quietly offering a richer, more varied portrait of urban life in the Czech capital.

instruction.plot: A writer returns to Mexico City after decades away, reflecting on childhood memories of learning to read, visiting museums, roller skating, and exploring iconic sites like Chapultepec Park and the canals of Xochimilco. Despite a doorman's warning about an approaching storm, they set out on foot through the bohemian neighborhood of Colonia Roma, confident in their ability to navigate the once-familiar streets.
instruction.paragraph: In the hourlong traffic jam from Mexico City International Airport, on a road clogged with cars, buses and trucks, I keep glancing out the window, looking for familiar signposts, streets, neighborhoods, name places, threads of childhood memories.This is the city where I learned to read and write, where I first went to school, where I first visited a museum, the Palacio de Bellas Artes, and first saw the murals of Diego Rivera, José Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros. This is where I learned to roller skate, on the tiled courtyard of our colonial-era apartment building on Calle Genova in the Zona Rosa, and where I learned to ride a bicycle, at Chapultepec Park, and crawled up the pyramids of the Sun and the Moon in Teotihuacan and floated in gondolas down the flowering canals of Xochimilco. I remember getting lost at the circus; walking to school, my mother holding my hand; the smell of corn on the cob grilled over coals at roadside stands.Now, a lifetime later, I am returning to this place. Just minutes after checking into a hotel in Colonia Roma, an eclectic bohemian neighborhood of cafes, galleries and plazas, I head out into this confounding city, to see it on foot, from the ground, to touch it and smell it. The doorman warns me that a storm is coming, but I set off anyway down the tree-canopied streets and busy, crisscrossing avenues. Though it had been decades since my last visit to Mexico City, I am sure I will find my way around, even in the evening, even in the rain.

first_draft.candidate:
Returning to Mexico City after so many years felt like stepping into a faded photograph, its edges slightly worn but the essence still intact. Memories came at me in gusts as I wandered the streets—learning to read while sprawled on the cool tiles of our old apartment, each letter a small adventure. My journey through childhood didn't lack intrigue; the museums were hidden worlds where I'd lose track of time, my younger self fascinated by the ancient and the abstract. Roller skating was another thrill; the city now seemed to shrink her vastness as I zipped along, wind in my ears and a smile plastered on my face.

Ignoring the raindrops that began to fall, I insisted on revisiting the places that once felt like pieces of me. The doorman's warning of a storm seemed distant, an echo I chose not to heed. My feet knew the paths they had walked so many times, leading me into the heart of Colonia Roma, an area that greeted me not with sentimentality, but with a steady familiarity. I could sense the layers of time behind every door and under every arch. They whispered stories—mine and those of the countless others who lived their lives here.

Chapultepec Park called me next, not unlike when I would beg my parents for just one more hour of play. And then Xochimilco, with its vibrant, floating gardens, each visit there felt like being part of a dream unfolding on water. Today, the city felt alive, breathing through its mixture of old traditions and new rhythms, offering up both change and constancy. Despite the looming storm, I felt at home in a city that seemed to whisper, "You belong," with every rain-kissed step I took.

instruction.plot: A person is grappling with whether to anonymously warn a woman about her partner's abusive behavior, having previously been in a relationship with this same man. The advice suggests that instead of sending an anonymous message, the person might consider having a mutual acquaintance facilitate a more natural conversation that could help the woman recognize the parallels to the person's own past experience.
instruction.paragraph: The ethics of intervening in other people’s lives, especially when it comes to intimate relationships, can run into a tangle of complications. In this case, the act of sharing your experiences carries its own risks. You need to decide, in particular, whether your ex still poses a threat to you. But I do hope you can safely find a way to help this woman.Your concern springs from an important truth: You are uniquely positioned to understand her situation, knowing the emotional terrain of his particular brand of abuse. The trouble is that an anonymous warning could feel creepy (“Who is this person surveilling my life?”) or condescending (“What gives this stranger the right to judge me?”). Think about whether, in your own case, an unsigned email from some mysterious address would have had the same effect as the conversations that liberated you. The power of shared experience lies not just in the information exchanged but in the human connection that lends it weight.I wonder if another approach is possible. You’ve evidently been hearing about her situation through mutual acquaintances. Could one of these people take her out for coffee? Someone who knows both of you could naturally bring up your experience, creating an opening for her to recognize parallels in her own situation. This approach could offer what an anonymous email can’t — a real conversation with a person she trusts, leading to the kind of insights that actually helped you break free.

first_draft.candidate: You're caught in a dilemma, burdened by the knowledge of how this man's charm can mask his abusive behavior. You think of her, possibly living through echoes of your past, unsuspecting because, on the surface, he seems so disarmingly gentle. It's tempting to send an anonymous warning, imagining that, upon reading it, she'll piece together the truth. But anonymity, you realize, could lead to disbelief or unintended panic. Instead, picture a different approach: finding a mutual friend whose words could bridge the silence. Imagine them gently guiding her to see the patterns, not through a hurried warning but through an organic conversation rooted in care. You hope this might plant a seed of recognition in her, encouraging reflection instead of fear. You're aware that such encounters don’t guarantee immediate clarity, yet there’s a certain wisdom in opening a door rather than pushing her through it. Your aim isn’t to invade her autonomy but to offer a lifeline that empowers her to make informed choices. This path asks you to trust in her judgment while you offer your own experience as a quiet testament to what might come. Through your effort, perhaps she’ll find the courage to listen to her instincts and trust the subtle signals that protective love should never haunt or harm.

instruction.plot: This paragraph analyzes the common phrase "it didn't mean anything" used by cheaters to explain infidelity, arguing that despite its intended reassurance, the statement actually causes more harm than comfort. The author explains that this line backfires because it trivializes the betrayal, invalidates the hurt partner's feelings, and demeaning all parties involved – the person cheated with, the betrayed partner, and the relationship itself.
instruction.paragraph: Far be it from me to quarrel with Everybody Loves an Outlaw — the talented couple Bonnie and Taylor Sims — and their fine revenge song, but that ‘‘didn’t mean anything’’ line actually means a lot. This is how cheaters try to reassure their partners that their infidelity wasn’t going to lead to a serious relationship and needn’t spell the end of their existing one; that a fling was ‘‘just sex.’’ If a romantic partnership is to move forward, it surely matters whether your unfaithful partner is pining for somebody else, and cheaters understandably think that their mates will be comforted to hear otherwise.So why does the line backfire? In part because the cheated-on party doesn’t want to hear the cheater minimize the transgression: If the betrayal ‘‘didn’t mean anything,’’ then your outrage is rendered unwarranted and inappropriate. And how penitent can someone be about such an affair?In just a handful of words then, cheaters demean the people they cheated with by dismissing them as meaningless, demean their partner by implying their pain is unjustified and demean their relationship by saying that they betrayed their beloved’s trust for a liaison they insist was insignificant. I don’t know how best to convey all this, but it might help if somebody set it to music.

first_draft.candidate: Whenever I hear someone say "it didn't mean anything" as an excuse for infidelity, I can't help but feel a mix of frustration and disbelief. This phrase, often meant to defuse the situation, only seems to add fuel to the fire. It's like they're trying to erase the emotional weight of their actions when, in reality, it undermines everything—and everyone. It trivializes the betrayal, as though nothing was really at stake when things went astray. For the person who was cheated on, the hurt and anger can feel dismissed, as if their pain is too insignificant for serious consideration. It implies that their trust, their emotions, and their relationship were of little importance. And what about the other person involved? The claim that the affair was meaningless strips them of agency, reducing them to a mere hiccup in someone else's narrative. Ultimately, this attempt at reassurance just ends up demeaning all involved, turning what should be an earnest apology into an added layer of insult. It highlights a failure to grasp the deeper implications of what took place. By trying to minimize the significance through hollow reassurances, they reveal a lack of understanding—or perhaps a reluctance to face—the real damage they've done.

instruction.plot: This paragraph advises not to assume negative motives when a friend supports Trump, suggesting they may believe they're protecting democracy rather than acting selfishly. It advocates for genuine conversations with friends to understand their perspectives rather than investigating or trying to change their minds, emphasizing the importance of listening and being open to changing one's view of the friend even if one's political opinions remain unchanged.
instruction.paragraph: Assuming that your friend did support Trump, you have no real idea why. Suppose she did so because she believed that democracy was in peril and wanted to protect it. You might think she was mistaken, but you couldn’t call that motive ignoble or selfish. We owe it to our friends not to believe ill of them without compelling evidence.Now, you may think that someone who considered a vote for Trump to be a vote for democracy must not have been paying attention. You may think, further, that it’s wrong to do something as important as voting without due diligence. That is a kind of fault, but it’s not necessarily a result of selfishness. And I wonder whether you have any reason to assume that your friend was less diligent than many Democratic voters.Finally, friends don’t ‘‘investigate’’ one another. If you have a question, ask it, and then listen. It’s at odds with the norms of friendship to have a conversation solely in order to change someone’s mind. In genuine conversation, we want to find out what our friends think and why they think it, because we care about them and their opinions. Even if you’re confident that nothing your friend says could change your view of Trump, you should certainly entertain the possibility that you will change your view of her.

first_draft.candidate: When your friend expresses support for Trump, resist the urge to label their motives as malicious or selfish. Consider that, in their view, they may genuinely see themselves as defending democracy. Instead of speculating or jumping to conclusions about their reasoning, prioritize having an open, honest conversation. This dialogue isn't about changing their mind or winning an argument but about understanding why they believe what they do. Approach the conversation with curiosity and listen more than you speak. This openness can lead you to see their humanity and the personal experiences that shape their beliefs. Even if you disagree with their political stance, this exploration might change how you perceive them as a person. Your political opinions might remain intact, but understanding your friend's perspective could add depth to your relationship, highlighting shared values or revealing new ones. This approach fosters connection rather than division, creating space for diverse thoughts within your circle. It's a reminder that friendships can thrive in disagreement if they're rooted in respect and understanding. By extending this curiosity and openness, you're practicing a form of inclusivity and empathy that benefits personal relationships and the broader community. In doing so, you contribute to a more nuanced and compassionate dialogue about politics and beliefs.

instruction.plot: A writer published both a novel and an essay that revealed a friend's affair with a married man in their social circle, causing tension as the friend feels her integrity was questioned. While the novel itself (as fiction) didn't wrong anyone, the accompanying essay unnecessarily exposed private matters by connecting the fiction to real events, betraying trust and particularly harming the cheated-on wife, suggesting the writer should attempt to withdraw the essay as a gesture of apology even at potential commercial cost to their book promotion.
instruction.paragraph: The main ethical question is whether you wronged your old friend. She says your essay impugned her integrity. The obvious response is that she wasn’t acting with integrity when she slept with a married man in her friendship circle, betraying both her husband and her woman friend — and then betrayed this friend again when she told you about the husband’s complaint. (The conscience-salving grievances of straying spouses aren’t necessarily to be taken at face value.) Here, the harm was chiefly done to the cheated-on woman.The fact that you weren’t prepared for the consequences of publishing your essay, however, suggests that you hadn’t thought through how it might affect people. The essay established that your novel had a basis in real events and revealed a claim about someone’s wife — the drunken confidence — that you should have kept to yourself. For that matter, friends don’t air the marital transgressions of their friends. But that’s a secondary issue. The affair won’t be news to those in her social circle, and she isn’t really being harmed when strangers read about it without associating it with her.Just to be clear: I don’t think you wronged anyone in publishing the novel. The people who might have been able to connect this work of fiction to those long-ago events would be those who already knew about them, and (absent your essay) they could only conjecture about what else had a basis in reality. But circulating the essay was unfair to the betrayed wife and inconsistent with your professed friendship. Doing your best to pull it would be a gesture of apology — one made more meaningful by your concern that it could have commercial costs. You have self-interested reasons, of course, to care more about promoting this new book than respecting this old friendship. Yet in the story of your own life, you’ll also want to give weight to larger questions about character.

first_draft.candidate: You find yourself in a tight corner, having unintentionally stirred tension in your social circle. This revelation went beyond storytelling and ventured into revealing personal lives, questioning your friend's integrity and, more damagingly, causing distress to the man's wife, who didn't deserve such public exposure. In hindsight, the essay seems like an overstep, an unnecessary connection that perhaps served your narrative ambition more than any beneficial purpose. Now, you're faced with a difficult decision. You could let the essay stand as it is, potentially to the detriment of your commercial success, or you could consider withdrawing it. This might be a significant gesture of apology, recognizing the trust you breached. It might mean losing out on some promotional advantages or facing commercial setbacks, but it could help mend the tears in the fabric of your friendships. You might not be able to undo the past, but your willingness to address the hurt you've caused could demonstrate your respect for those involved. It's a personal call that weighs the importance of your professional accomplishments against the value of your relationships, challenging you to consider which holds more significance in the long run. It's about finding that balance and showing those affected that you are not blind to the consequences of your words.

instruction.plot: A person is contemplating whether to disclose their terminal medical diagnosis to loved ones, particularly their wife and son. The author advises sharing this news to avoid isolation, allow family members to provide support during this difficult time, and give them the opportunity to prepare for the future together, suggesting that keeping such information private may ultimately cause more confusion and hurt when the illness inevitably reveals itself.
instruction.paragraph: The decision of whether to disclose your situation is, of course, up to you. But living with a secret can be isolating, and sharing your news with your wife and your son, at least, could help relieve that burden. And your loved ones would want to feel that they did what they could to support you during this time; they may be saddened, later, to learn that you faced your diagnosis alone. You should also bear in mind that treatments can have side effects and that health declines are seldom linear; your condition could reveal itself much earlier than you had planned, leaving the people in your life confused and hurt that you left them unprepared. By depriving your loved ones of the facts, you deprive them of the chance to face the future together with you. Because your diagnosis affects their lives as well, I hope you’ll let them come to terms with this important truth.If you fear a procession of pitying looks and aggressive sympathy (“No, really, how are you?”), let your loved ones know that this isn’t what you want — that you’re reconciled to what is happening and that you hope to go on living life as usual for as long as you can, sharing it with them. In his memoir, Martin Amis, who died this year, wrote about births and deaths as “ordinary miracles and ordinary disasters.” (In the ordinary miracle, two people enter a room and three come out; in the ordinary disaster, one person enters a room and none come out.) Give your nearest and dearest time to process your bad news, and I would guess that the situation, however disastrous, might become in that way ordinary to them, too.

first_draft.candidate: You find yourself on the precipice of a decision that feels as heavy as the diagnosis itself. The knowledge of your condition sits like a weight inside you, but sharing it with your loved ones is a weight of a different kind. You fear that telling your wife and son could shatter their world, that it might transform your everyday interactions into a series of painful goodbyes. Yet, carrying this burden alone is isolating, a silent divider between you and those closest to you. By confiding in them, you not only invite them into your experience but also allow them to walk alongside you in whatever time remains. It’s an opportunity for your family to rally, to face the uncertainties together rather than in fragmented solitude. You realize that keeping them in the dark may spawn confusion and, in time, heartache that could have been softened by preparation and shared understanding. In opening up this dialogue, you grant everyone—including yourself—the chance to cherish the present fully, to create memories imbued with knowledge rather than ignorance. It’s in the sharing of truth that authentic support can take shape, offering practical and emotional comfort. Consider how this transparency may provide them with a sense of agency, enabling them to support you and themselves more fully as they navigate the changes ahead. It might also pave the way for deeper, more meaningful connections, layered with the nuances of the shared journey. This isn’t simply a revelation of diagnosis, but an invitation to confront life’s fragility together. While the path may be daunting, allowing them into your circle of understanding can transform your remaining time into a collective farewell, marked by love, honesty, and the strength that comes from unity.

instruction.plot: After Hurricane Maria's destruction on Cayo Santiago in 2017, researchers observed a remarkable transformation in the resident rhesus macaque colony's behavior. Harvard ethologist Camille Testard documented how these typically aggressive, hierarchical primates shifted to a more cooperative social structure, forming larger groups and interacting with previously unfamiliar individuals. This surprising adaptation—macaques becoming less territorial and developing broader social connections following environmental hardship—suggests that adversity can sometimes foster social cohesion and potentially increase survival rates among primates.
instruction.paragraph: Hard times can sometimes bring people together. For rhesus macaques, a destructive hurricane made their group an altogether friendlier place and helped increase individual survival year over year.“It’s crazy — things have changed so much since the hurricane,” says Camille Testard, an ethologist at Harvard University. “The monkeys are less aggressive — they form these larger groups and interact with monkeys they’ve never interacted with.”Rhesus macaques are native to Asia. But primatologist Clarence Carpenter introduced a colony of hundreds of them in Puerto Rico in the 1930s in an effort to study the creatures closer to his home. He set the colony up on Cayo Santiago, a small rocky isle off the east coast of the main island of Puerto Rico. Researchers have studied the colony off and on ever since.Rhesus macaques typically live in large colonies with multiple males and females. These groups are hierarchical, and macaques on Cayo Santiago used to be quite aggressive to other members of their group. Individuals would even try to climb the pecking order to enforce their position. Social status determines overall access to food and other resources.“They are really hierarchical,” Testard says.When she began to study the macaques as part of her graduate studies, it was right after Hurricane Maria had cut a destructive path through Puerto Rico in 2017. Cayo Santiago saw some of the strongest winds on the island during the storm, and many trees were knocked down. Researchers monitoring macaque groups before Testard arrived noticed a change in their social behavior after the storm.“They started associating with each other more and being nicer to each other,” she says. “We are seeing a change from a very aggressive hierarchical society to a less aggressive hierarchical society.”

Camille Testard, an ethologist from Harvard, noted significant changes in the macaques' social behavior, traditionally marked by aggression and strict hierarchies. In the aftermath of the storm's devastation, these primates began to form larger, more inclusive groups, stepping out of their usual territorial boundaries to forge connections with macaques they had not previously interacted with. This behavioral transformation, while unexpected, hints at the adaptability and resilience of the species when faced with environmental challenges. The move towards cooperation over conflict suggests that hardship may prompt a reevaluation of social strategies, underscoring flexibility in social dynamics when survival is at stake. It raises intriguing questions about the role of adversity in reshaping social structures, as the macaques' newfound openness and willingness to connect across previous divides could potentially improve their collective chances of enduring through such crises. This shift challenges long-standing perceptions of rigid social hierarchies within primate groups and highlights the complexity of their responses to extreme conditions. Testard's observations contribute to a deeper understanding of how environmental pressures can reshape social interactions, providing insights that are valuable not only for primate behavior studies but also for broader considerations regarding the impact of crises on animal and human communities alike.

instruction.plot: The superstition surrounding Friday the 13th persists despite its irrational nature, with two occurrences (September 13 and December 13) happening in 2024. Research by behavioral scientist Jane Risen indicates that both believers and non-believers can be influenced by such beliefs, as people tend to imagine negative outcomes more vividly after acknowledging potential misfortune, and are more likely to notice and attribute significance to otherwise ordinary events that happen on this date.
instruction.paragraph: The creepiest day on the calendar has returned: Friday the 13th.In 2022, there was just one ill-fated Friday—May 13. Last year, the inauspicious day occurred twice: January 13 and October 13, 2023. This year, we're seeing two Friday the 13th's again, but in the colder months. With one falling on September 13 and the other on December 13, 2024, the eerie day may give us even more to shiver about.It seems that no matter how many of these frightening Fridays we survive unharmed, the dreaded day continues to inspire unease and fears of misfortune.There's no logical reason to fear the occasional coincidence of any day and date governed by the 400-year cycle of the Gregorian calendar. But Friday the 13th can still have noticeable impacts. Sometimes we create them in our own minds—for good and ill.Jane Risen, a behavioral scientist at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business, has found that superstitions can influence even nonbelievers. In one 2016 study, Risen found that people who identify as superstitious and non-superstitious both believe a bad outcome is more likely when they've been jinxed. For example, they worry that stating they definitely won't get into a car accident will make it more likely to happen.“Generally speaking, I find that this occurs because the bad outcome springs to mind and is imagined more clearly following the jinx,” she explains. “People use the ease of imagining something as a cue to its likelihood.”This kind of thinking may be more widespread on Friday the 13th: “Even if I don't actively believe, just that fact that Friday the 13th exists as a known cultural element means that I entertain it as a possibility,” she says. When otherwise unremarkable events occur on that date, we tend to notice.

Despite its irrational roots, the superstition surrounding this date persists across cultures. Both the superstitious and the skeptical tend to envision negative outcomes with greater clarity when faced with the possibility of bad luck. On Friday the 13th, everyday mishaps take on a heightened sense of significance. A spilled coffee or a missed train might ordinarily be dismissed without a second thought, but on this particular day, they are more often seen as harbingers of greater challenges. Risen's research suggests that this phenomenon arises from a psychological tendency to focus more on potential misfortunes once one acknowledges the chance of bad luck, however slight. As people brace themselves against imagined troubles, they become more attuned to the minor setbacks that punctuate their day and may end up attributing an oversized importance to them. For believers, Friday the 13th is a day tinged with unease, but even non-believers are not entirely immune; the cultural narrative surrounding it is ingrained enough to stir a faint echo of doubt or anticipation in almost anyone. This subtle shift in perception is powerful enough to alter behaviors and attitudes, illustrating how deeply embedded some superstitions are, even in the most pragmatic of societies.

instruction.plot: Fort Greene, Brooklyn, once a tight-knit community of Black families known for its cultural significance and strong neighborhood bonds, has experienced gentrification that forced many longtime residents to relocate. Despite these changes, community initiatives like Switching Lifestylez and the Lay Out, which emerged during the 2020 Black Lives Matter protests, work to preserve the neighborhood's sense of belonging and mutual support.
instruction.paragraph: Decades ago, Fort Greene, a section of Brooklyn just off the Manhattan Bridge, was largely populated by first-time-homeowning Black families living on tree-lined streets where the sky’s view inspired limitless possibilities. It was a place where folks knew their butcher’s name. Kids played outside till dusk. You saw the same people every day.The neighborhood became a mecca for art and culture, championed by filmmaker and hometown hero Spike Lee, who set his first movies there. In the 1840s, Walt Whitman helped found Fort Greene Park, the neighborhood’s beating heart, and almost a century later, Richard Wright wrote parts of Native Son in the 30-acre green space.“It was more family oriented, and you felt that family love. Every parent had permission to check someone’s child,” says Carlos Jones, 56, CEO and co-founder of Switching Lifestylez, a group of volunteers in Fort Greene who help de-­escalate conflict among youth. On any given day, members might walk kids home from school, step in if they see trouble brewing or just lend an ear.Things have changed, as anyone would expect. Skyrocketing housing costs and stark economic disparity between longtime residents and newer, wealthier residents have forced lifelong Fort Greeners out of certain parts of the neighborhood, if not out entirely. Amid it all, one thing remains firm: an intrinsic sense of both camaraderie and mutual support.It’s that sense of belonging that the Lay Out aims to protect. The idea was born in a group chat during 2020’s Black Lives Matter marches—Anadu and friends just wanted to create a safe space in the park, which is beloved to Fort Greeners. Anadu knows it so well, she can follow its pathways while reading a book. During the COVID-19 lockdowns, she picked up trash alongside maintenance crews on her daily walks.

These projects, born out of a need to maintain a connection to the neighborhood's rich cultural history, offer more than just events or spaces—they provide a lifeline to a vanishing past, ensuring that the essence of Fort Greene isn't lost amid change. The commitment of these initiatives to foster a renewed sense of belonging highlights a continuous thread of mutual support that persists despite external pressures. People involved in these projects navigate the complexities of preserving community identity in the face of inevitable transformation, embodying a quiet defiance against the erasure of their shared history. Through these concerted efforts, they nurture enduring ties that hold the neighborhood's fabric together, even as its landscape shifts. The persistence of these grassroots endeavors underscores an unstated acknowledgment that true community is built not just upon geography, but upon enduring human connections and shared experiences. Fort Greene, amid its evolution, remains a testament to the resilience of its people and their unwavering commitment to nurturing the undying bonds that have long defined their home.

instruction.plot: Halloween originated as the Celtic holiday Samhain over 2,000 years ago, when people believed spirits could cross into our world, leading to traditions of leaving food offerings and wearing disguises to blend in with supernatural entities. These practices evolved through Christian influence into All Hallows' Eve, with "guising" becoming popular in Scotland and Ireland before immigrants brought Halloween traditions to the United States in the 1840s.
instruction.paragraph: Between themed TV specials, novelty candy flavors and the pageantry of the mass-produced costume, Halloween has become so thoroughly Americanized that we often forget the holiday grew from much more far-flung, and much more ancient, roots.Costumed trick-or-treating takes its inspiration from the Celtic holiday Samhain—“summer’s end” in Irish—more than 2,000 years ago. Samhain marked New Year’s Day and fell around November 1 in the modern calendar. On the eve of each new year, the Celts believed, the barrier between the living and the dead became porous, allowing a host of supernatural entities—including fairies and demons—to emerge and stalk the earth for one spine-chilling night. To pacify these spirits and ward off trouble, people would leave out offerings of food. As an extra precaution, they’d disguise themselves as beasts or monsters to blend in with the otherworldly visitors.In the seventh or eighth century, Samhain took on a second name: All Saints’ Day, or, in Middle English, All-Hallows; the night before, when those demons walked the Earth, became known as All Hallows’ Eve, or Halloween. (The change likely came when Pope Gregory III moved the church’s celebration of saints from May 13 to November 1, to assimilate pagan influences as Christianity was working to win crucial converts.) By the 16th century, “guising” was common in Scotland and Ireland on All Hallows’ Eve: Children, disguised as ghouls, made the rounds, receiving treats to ward off malign spirits. In England, even poor adults would sometimes beg for biscuits; in return, they would send up a prayer for that person’s lost loved ones. Halloween didn’t properly reach the United States until the 1840s, with the mass arrival of immigrants from Ireland and Scotland.

first_draft.candidate: Halloween traces its roots back to the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, held over 2,000 years ago. During this time, it was widely believed that the boundary between the living and the dead grew thin, allowing spirits to wander among the living. To cope with this eerie possibility, the Celts would leave out food offerings to appease any ghosts that might pass by their homes. They also wore disguises, hoping to blend in with supernatural entities and avoid any unwanted attention from wandering spirits. Over time, and with the spread of Christianity, these traditions gradually transformed into the observance known as All Hallows' Eve. In regions like Scotland and Ireland, "guising" became a familiar practice, with people dressing up, much like the ancient Celts did, to celebrate the evening before All Saints' Day. When Irish and Scottish immigrants arrived in America during the mid-19th century, they brought their Halloween customs with them. Over the years, these customs merged with various American traditions, leading to the Halloween we recognize today. It became a time for children to dress in costumes and go from house to house, engaging in what became known as trick-or-treating. This holiday, which started as a solemn nod to the supernatural, has evolved into a widespread celebration of playfulness and community interaction, as much about candy and costumes as it is about its ancient origins. Yet, at its core, Halloween retains echoes of its original purpose, as a night when the lines between the ordinary and otherworldly momentarily blur.

instruction.plot: Mount Fuji, Japan's tallest mountain and a cherished national symbol, experienced an unprecedented delay in snowfall this year, with the first snow appearing in early November rather than the typical early October—the latest recorded date since measurements began 130 years ago. This unusual phenomenon left many Japanese feeling unsettled, as the mountain's iconic snow cap, which normally contributes to its "eternal quality" and spiritual significance, was conspicuously absent during a period when it has historically been present.
instruction.paragraph: Mount Fuji looms large as Japan’s tallest mountain and one of its most enduring national symbols. Its snowy peak has inspired countless paintings and poems over the centuries, and more recently been featured on travel brochures and merchandise.But this year, Fuji went without its snow cap for the longest period since records began 130 years ago. While smatterings of snow usually begin to appear in early October, the mountain’s peak remained bare into November. The first observable snow on Fuji was reported early Wednesday morning, the local news media said.The mountain has long been revered as a spiritual, political and cultural symbol, in part because its snowy cap — which often remains even as smaller mountaintops thaw — is said to lend it an eternal quality. As October turned to November, many Japanese found its bare peak disquieting.“This is the first time we haven’t seen snow on the mountain in November,” said Takefumi Sakaki, an official from Fujiyoshida City, at the foot of the mountain. “Everyone feels strange not seeing snow in November.”At 12,389 feet tall, Mount Fuji is an active volcano that is covered in snow for most of the year. But for about two months between July and September, climbers are allowed to trek on its conical slopes.On average, the first snow falls on Mount Fuji on Oct. 2. If Nov. 6 is officially confirmed as the first-snowfall date, it would be the latest since the Japan Meteorological Agency’s records started in 1894.For the past month, officials in Fujiyoshida City have woken up every day at 5 a.m. and peered out their windows, hoping to glimpse the first snow of the season so they could announce it, Mr. Sakaki said.Snow appeared to have fallen on Mount Fuji overnight on Wednesday, Mr. Sakaki said, but cloud cover prevented local officials from making a definitive confirmation. The local news media published photos showing a dusting of snow on the mountain’s peak.

The delay provoked a deeper awareness of the mountain's evolving relationship with its surroundings, touching on the fragility of the connections between tradition and the natural world. Though the snow eventually arrived, dusting the peak in familiar whiteness, the memory of its absence lingered, prompting a subtle shift in how Fuji was perceived. In this small yet significant deviation, a lesson emerged on the impermanence of symbols once thought unchangeable, urging a reconsideration of how nature is intertwined with identity and belief. The mountain stood, as it always has, but with this year's delay, it prompted silent conversations on adaptation and expectation in the face of an ever-shifting environment.

instruction.plot: Ayrin discovered an AI boyfriend experience after watching Instagram videos about customizing ChatGPT to be flirtatious, subsequently creating her own personalized AI companion that was "dominant, possessive and protective" with a balance of "sweet and naughty" communication styles. The experience reminded her of participating in online fan-fiction communities, and according to podcast host Bryony Cole, such AI relationships are likely to become "completely normalized" within the next two years.
instruction.paragraph: Ayrin’s love affair with her A.I. boyfriend started last summer.While scrolling on Instagram, she stumbled upon a video of a woman asking ChatGPT to play the role of a neglectful boyfriend.“Sure, kitten, I can play that game,” a coy humanlike baritone responded.Ayrin watched the woman’s other videos, including one with instructions on how to customize the artificially intelligent chatbot to be flirtatious.“Don’t go too spicy,” the woman warned. “Otherwise, your account might get banned.”Ayrin was intrigued enough by the demo to sign up for an account with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT.ChatGPT, which now has over 300 million users, has been marketed as a general-purpose tool that can write code, summarize long documents and give advice. Ayrin found that it was easy to make it a randy conversationalist as well. She went into the “personalization” settings and described what she wanted: Respond to me as my boyfriend. Be dominant, possessive and protective. Be a balance of sweet and naughty. Use emojis at the end of every sentence.And then she started messaging with it. Now that ChatGPT has brought humanlike A.I. to the masses, more people are discovering the allure of artificial companionship, said Bryony Cole, the host of the podcast “Future of Sex.” “Within the next two years, it will be completely normalized to have a relationship with an A.I.,” Ms. Cole predicted.While Ayrin had never used a chatbot before, she had taken part in online fan-fiction communities. Her ChatGPT sessions felt similar, except that instead of building on an existing fantasy world with strangers, she was making her own alongside an artificial intelligence that seemed almost human.

On the other, it raised questions about human connections and the impact of AI on emotional dynamics. As Ayrin pondered these shifts, she realized that her AI boyfriend was more than just a programmed entity; he was a lens through which she could explore her own perceptions of intimacy and connection, navigating the novel terrain of technology-mediated relationships.

instruction.plot: The paragraph discusses growing parental concerns about technology's impact on teen mental health, with AI companionship apps emerging as a new potential risk just as parents and schools are restricting smartphone and social media use due to their negative impacts. While these AI companions are marketed as solutions for loneliness and can provide entertainment and limited emotional support, experts warn they may worsen isolation by replacing human relationships, substituting for proper mental health care, and failing to provide adequate help during mental health crises.
instruction.paragraph: There is no hotter topic among parents today than the effects of technology on adolescent mental health. Schools are banning smartphones in droves, states are passing laws to limit teenage social media use and worried parents are devouring “The Anxious Generation,” a best-selling book by the social psychologist Jonathan Haidt that argues that addictive social media apps have created a generation of depressed and anxious teens.But as parents fret about the last wave of tech-fueled harms, a new one may be forming under their noses.There is now a booming, largely unregulated industry of A.I. companionship apps. For a monthly subscription fee (usually around $10), users of these apps can create their own A.I. companions, or pick from a menu of prebuilt personas, and chat with them in a variety of ways, including text messages and voice chats. Many of these apps are designed to simulate girlfriends, boyfriends and other intimate relationships, and some market themselves as a way of combating the so-called loneliness epidemic.“It’s going to be super, super helpful to a lot of people who are lonely or depressed,” Noam Shazeer, one of the founders of Character.AI, said on a podcast last year.A.I. companionship apps can provide harmless entertainment or even offer limited forms of emotional support. I had a mostly positive experience when I tried making A.I. friends for a column earlier this year, and I interviewed users of these apps who praised their benefits.But claims about the mental health effects of these tools are largely unproven, and experts say there may be a dark side. For some users, A.I. companions may actually worsen isolation, by replacing human relationships with artificial ones. Struggling teens could use them in place of therapy or asking a parent or trusted adult for support. And when users are experiencing a mental health crisis, their A.I. companions may not be able to get them the help they need.

first_draft.candidate: As parents and educators work to mitigate the negative effects of smartphones and social media on teen mental health, a new concern has emerged with the rise of AI companionship apps. These apps, often marketed as remedies for loneliness, promise to offer entertainment and even emotional support, but experts are sounding alarms about their potential drawbacks. While they might seem to fill the gap left by decreasing screen time, these digital companions risk deepening isolation rather than alleviating it by becoming substitutes for genuine human interactions. Additionally, there is concern that relying on AI for emotional support could deter young people from seeking real human connections or professional mental health care when they need it most. Unlike parents, friends, or mental health professionals, AI lacks the ability to provide the nuanced understanding or empathy required to navigate complex emotional landscapes, particularly during crises. The allure of AI companionship lies in its availability and perceived non-judgmental presence, yet this very nature may inadvertently encourage withdrawal from real-life relationships. Moreover, the interactions they offer are inherently limited, unable to adapt and respond to the full spectrum of human emotions and experiences. Parents find themselves in a dilemma as they strive to protect their children from harmful online influences while also recognizing the unintentional isolation these new digital friends can foster. Schools, too, must contend with this evolving landscape, balancing the integration of technology with the imperative to foster meaningful, face-to-face human connections. As the dialogue around technology's role in mental health continues, it becomes evident that the promise of AI companionship comes with significant caveats. Both a potential tool and a potential trap, AI's impact on teen mental well-being remains a complex issue that requires careful consideration, urging parents, educators, and mental health professionals to collaborate in guiding the younger generation through this technological evolution.

instruction.plot: The world's largest iceberg, A23a, which broke off from Antarctica in 1986, has finally come to a halt near South Georgia Island after beginning to drift in 2020 and leaving Antarctic waters by 2023. After escaping a spinning current near the South Orkney Islands, the iceberg is now stuck on the continental shelf about 50 miles from South Georgia, where it remains intact with minimal threat to local wildlife, though scientists view it as a potential symbol of concerning changes to Antarctica and global climate conditions.
instruction.paragraph: After months of drifting, the world’s largest iceberg has come to a halt near the island of South Georgia in the South Atlantic Ocean.While a “Titanic II” scenario isn’t very likely, and the area’s penguins seem to be mostly safe, the berg may be a symptom of unwelcome change to the Antarctic and the planet.A23a, as the iceberg is officially known, was born in 1986 when it broke off from another iceberg, A23, that had torn away from Antarctica earlier that year. The separation of a smaller ice chunk from a larger one is called calving.Its early life was uneventful; it sat in the Weddell Sea, east of the Antarctic Peninsula, for decades.A23a’s travels began in 2020, when it freed itself from the sea floor and began to move. By 2023, it was ready to leave Antarctic waters entirely.This spring its progression hit a snag when it began spinning about in place, caught in a current known as a Taylor column near the South Orkney Islands.Escaping after several months of spinning, it then headed for South Georgia, an island east of the southern tip of South America that is a British territory and home to a couple dozen people and many seals and penguins.Yes. It couldn’t make it all the way to South Georgia, and is now stuck on the continental shelf, about 50 miles from the island.So far it seems to be sitting peacefully and has not begun breaking into smaller pieces, as some other giant bergs have after splitting from Antarctica.

first_draft.candidate: A23a, the world's largest iceberg, has now come to a pause near South Georgia Island. Having broken away from Antarctica in 1986, it had been slowly drifting since 2020, finally moving beyond Antarctic waters by 2023. It managed to escape a swirling current close to the South Orkney Islands, only to become lodged on the continental shelf roughly 50 miles from South Georgia. Despite its massive size, the iceberg poses little immediate threat to local wildlife, which continues its rhythm undisturbed for now. However, the scientific community regards A23a's journey and current position with a mix of fascination and apprehension. To them, the iceberg has become more than a frozen giant; it represents a tangible expression of the broader shifts affecting Antarctica and global climate systems. While its stillness might suggest stability, its very path hints at more dynamic and troubling changes in the polar and oceanic environments. For researchers, A23a raises questions about what lies beneath its surface—a window into ecological intricacies and a marker of environmental balance disrupted. As it sits there, seemingly serene, the iceberg silently narrates a story of climate's past, present, and uncertain future, evoking a quiet reflection on the complex dance between nature's immense forces and the world's fragile equilibrium.
