instruction.plot: "Til There Was You" is a 90s romantic comedy where ghostwriter Gwen (Jeanne Tripplehorn) anonymously writes passionate newspaper letters protesting the demolition of her historic apartment building, La Fortuna, unknowingly charming the very architect, Nick (Dylan McDermott), who's been hired to replace it with high-rise condos. Nick eventually falls for the anonymous writer's passion for preserving the bohemian community, breaks up with his girlfriend (Sarah Jessica Parker), and races to find the woman behind the letters while convincing his firm to save the building.
instruction.paragraph: In the late nineties, a movie came out about a slick-talking, hot-shot developer who is about to destroy a small but cherished neighborhood institution when he reads the letters of a woman who’s trying to save it and falls in love with her. I’m not talking about “You’ve Got Mail,” Nora Ephron’s classic ode to indie bookstores and Upper West Side quaintness. I’m referring to the box-office bomb “ ’Til There Was You,” an agitprop rom-com about zoning laws written by Winnie Holzman, the creator of “My So-Called Life.” In the film, Jeanne Tripplehorn plays Gwen, a struggling ghostwriter looking to rent a place in Los Angeles. She finds an apartment in La Fortuna, a historic building—based on the real-life El Cabrillo condominium in Hollywood—where a bohemian, multigenerational coterie of residents gathers in a shared courtyard to smoke, play music, and reminisce about old flames. Gwen keeps to herself, though; this is just a “temporary shelter” until she moves to New York City to be a real writer. instruction.plot: The author reflects on her Israeli childhood watching "Hahaverim Shel Yael," where her mother, a philosophy professor, questioned the host's instruction to "Tell your mother to turn up the volume" by asking "And what about those who don't have a mother?"—initially irritating the author but later revealing her mother's thoughtful approach to parenting. Years after her mother's death, the author appreciates how her mother treated her and her twin sister as thoughtful people capable of empathy, demonstrated a unique sense of fairness centered on children's needs rather than strict equality, and expressed love by cleverly telling each twin she loved her "more" when asked who was the favorite.
instruction.paragraph: When I was growing up, in Israel, there was a short-lived show on television called “Hahaverim Shel Yael” (“Yael’s Friends”), which featured a peppy girl who introduced short clips acted out by puppets. The actress who played Yael was probably in her twenties, but she was dressed up to look like a child, in flowery dresses and pigtails. I loved that program, in which the puppets occasionally crossed into real life and made a mess of Yael’s studio. Right before the opening music came on, Yael would look into the camera and fake-whisper to the viewers, “Tell your mother to turn up the volume!” Once, as my twin sister and I were settling down on the sofa to watch, my mother overheard this opening bit. “And what about those who don’t have a mother?” she asked.I must have been seven or eight at the time. I was irritated with her for asking that question, forever ruining the show for me. But I shouldn’t have been surprised. It summed up, I now realize, her parenting philosophy. The way she didn’t baby us, but treated us like thoughtful people, capable of empathy. The way she was always fully there—registering, questioning. But mostly, I think, it showed her unyielding belief in fairness, which, years later, I would hear her define as justice played out in the private sphere. (She was a philosophy professor, preoccupied with definitions.) It was a particular kind of fairness, one that centered on a child’s sensibility. Once, when I asked her whom she loved more, my sister or me, she answered, simply, “You.” Incredulous, my sister posed the same question. “Who do you love more, Ima? Ruth or me?” “You,” my mother said. We tried again. Each time, my mother invariably told whoever asked that she loved her more. “This doesn’t make any sense,” we finally said. She smiled and told us, “Sure it does. Don’t you see? I love you more and I love you more.” This was her sense of fairness: no kid wants to hear that she is loved the same as her sister.This Mother’s Day, three and a half years after she died, I find myself turning over her question in my mind. And what about those who don’t have a mother?

first_draft.candidate:
Growing up in Israel, my world was often colored by the vibrant sensations I absorbed from TV, particularly "Hahaverim Shel Yael." Each episode felt like a lively invitation to engage with the colorful universe presented on the screen. Yet, for my mother, a philosophy professor more comfortable challenging deep-seated assumptions than indulging in children's television, even such simple directives as "Tell your mother to turn up the volume" were subject to scrutiny. I remember the first time she questioned it with a gentle yet probing, "And what about those who don't have a mother?" Her words initially felt more like an irritation than an insight; couldn't we just enjoy the show without complicating it? Looking back, though, I see this was just one instance of her thoughtful approach unraveling before me, like the first clue in a lifelong mystery of understanding. Her questioning wasn't only philosophical but deeply caring, revealing an empathy that extended beyond our family to consider unseen others, an empathy she infused in our upbringing.

After my mother's death, memories like these have become treasured puzzles I piece together, drawing connections I once overlooked. Her approach to parenting defied the straightforward rules typical of most families around us. My twin sister and I learned early on that fairness, according to her, meant prioritizing each child's needs, an approach that held its own compass distinct from mere equality. This principle showed itself in the profound fairness she practiced daily, one that resonated more with feelings than measurable fairness—things might not be equal, but they were right for us individually. When we pressed her with that age-old question of favoritism, her eyes twinkled with a clever sort of love as she assured me and my sister separately, "I love you more." At the time, it seemed like little more than a humorous deflection, yet it perfectly encapsulated her belief that love wasn't a finite resource to be divided. Now, those words echo in my heart, a testament to how she embraced us as thoughtful people, weaving empathy and humor into a legacy of love and understanding that I carry forward.

instruction.plot: In 2003, a military friend rescues a pregnant stray cat at Fort Bragg, later distributing the "military-grade" kittens (known for fetching, coming when called, and strategically puking on non-porous surfaces) to the narrator and their parents, with the narrator's kitten surviving for twenty-one years until falling gravely ill. Now, as the narrator awaits a veterinarian's arrival to euthanize their beloved cat, they reflect on their long journey together and privately believe the cat's exceptional longevity demonstrates the power of nurture, while recalling the family joke about their tax dollars producing these remarkable felines.
instruction.paragraph: It’s 2003 and a childhood friend is stationed at Fort Bragg, in North Carolina—which will be renamed Fort Liberty in 2023—where she’s in the 82nd Airborne Division. She is done jumping out of planes for the day, heading off the base, when she hears meowing coming from a warehouse. Inside, she finds a stray cat, proud but mangy, and decides to take her home. The cat is pregnant. My friend e-mails me a photograph of the kittens, arranged on her lap, one surfing on her kneecap. She writes, “Don’t these remind you of your cats growing up?” She knows a target when she sees one.A few weeks later, the kittens are loaded onto the back seat of a Jeep and driven north. Two are dropped off at my parents’ house, in White Plains, and one is dropped off with me at my studio apartment, on the Upper West Side. The family joke is that these are military-grade cats. Your tax dollars at work. No laser eyes, but they do fetch and come when you call them, and, if they puke, they do so on nonporous surfaces. Twenty-one years later, mine is the last one standing. Personally, I think there’s a lesson here about nurture, but I keep this thought to myself.The cat is very sick, so a veterinarian whom I have never met is coming over to kill her. She arrives at 10 A.M., which feels wrong. Murders and breakups, these are not interactions for God’s hours. On the phone the afternoon before, she tells me of her pastoral childhood in New Zealand. Her mother once put a cat down by feeding it Valium.

I got one of those kittens, and here we are, twenty-one years later, waiting for the vet to arrive. It's hard to believe how much time has passed and how much we’ve shared. As I lie next to my cat, who’s now gravely ill, my mind drifts back over the years. Maybe it’s sentiment, but I like to think her extraordinary lifespan is a testament to the nurturing she received, rather than just her impressive genetic start. My family always joked that our tax dollars were well spent if they produced such remarkable creatures—but tucked within that humor was a real sense of marvel and affection. Those years turned what started as a playful exaggeration into something closer to a truth we all cherished. Today, those jokes feel like a thin veil over a deeper understanding of what she meant, not just to me, but to my whole family. Sitting quietly, I find solace in knowing that every moment shared—each purr, every quirk—was colored by the life we built together. As the vet's arrival draws near, I'm filled with gratitude for the years I’ve had with her and the subtle lessons she taught, far beyond her amusing "military-grade" antics. In this quiet space, I hold onto the idea that nurture sculpted something precious out of the raw potential we once joked about.

instruction.plot: At a rave in March 2020, the narrator and Andrew shared LSD-infused water before the party, with the narrator contemplating a book about the Amazon rainforest while experiencing the drug's effects. The night, which would later become memorable for unspecified reasons, occurred during the early days of COVID-19 awareness, as evidenced by the narrator's previous cautious movie theater experience where people were avoiding touching surfaces and being conscious of coughs.
instruction.paragraph: On March 6, 2020, Andrew and I went to a rave. If it weren’t for what happened later, I don’t think it would have stood out in my memory. A couple of days before, I had met a friend at the movie theatre at the Brooklyn Academy of Music, to see “Portrait of a Lady on Fire.” It was the first time I saw someone trying to open a door with his elbows. My friend and I ordered separate popcorns as a hygienic precaution. I remember someone behind us coughing, and being aware of it.On Friday night, before the party, I put a single drop of LSD into a glass of water. I drank half, and Andrew drank the other half. For the next couple of hours, while he made beats in his studio, I lay in bed with my eyes closed, listening to one of the final mixes made by Andrew Weatherall, a British d.j. who had got his start in the nineteen-eighties club scene and had recently died. The tracks had titles like “Jagged Mountain Melts at Dawn” and “The Descending Moonshine Dervishes.”I sat up in bed, and, as the waves of acid broke over me, I wrote down some thoughts. I was a magazine writer, but I was thinking of going to Brazil to write a book about the Amazon rain forest. The problem with trying to write a book about the Amazon rain forest was that it was a place that was much better left alone, like Everest, or the moon. I looked over at the cat, who was sitting on an ottoman, her eyes two glowing lamps of annoyance. It was time to go out.

first_draft.candidate: On that night in March 2020, my mind was already straddling two worlds before the LSD kicked in. The buzz of the party surrounded us, but my thoughts kept drifting to a book I'd been reading about the Amazon rainforest—about how vast and unknowable it seemed, much like the uncharted territory we were stepping into with the news of COVID-19 spreading. Andrew handed me the bottle of water, and as I drank, I felt the liquid flow through me, almost like it was carrying us to a different plane. The room started to shift subtly, colors popping and merging in unexpected ways. I recalled the anxious vibe at the movie theater earlier that week, where people avoided touching surfaces and kept tabs on their own coughs, a newfound hyper-awareness settling over us all. But in the pulsating heart of the rave, that unease seemed to temporarily wash away, replaced with a kinetic, shared abandon as we let the music carry us. Little did I know, this night would imprint itself in my memory, not just for the psychedelic trip or its timing in a world on the brink of profound change, but for reasons that only revealed themselves later. The Amazon, like the future unfolding before us, loomed large in my mind—the mystery of both stretching out in ways I couldn't yet decipher.

instruction.plot: A teenage girl, obsessed with writing detailed funeral orations that identify who should feel guilty for her death without actually having suicidal intentions, falls thirty feet from her bedroom window on April 16, 1993. In these imagined scenarios, she envisions her tormentors—from "skinny bitches with straight hair" to a "sadistic French teacher"—finally recognizing her worth and inner beauty, though she takes satisfaction in knowing their realizations would come too late.
instruction.paragraph: Many interesting things have happened to adult me, but in the opinion of teen-age me there is only one real event in our lives and it occurred on the sixteenth of April, 1993, when I fell thirty feet from my bedroom window. I need to give backstory. (Teen-age me was obsessed with backstory.) Prior to the fall, I had spent a couple of years periodically writing long orations to be read out at my funeral. (By whom? My brothers?) The purpose of these speeches was to explain to the congregation exactly why teen-age me had decided to leave this world, and who, precisely, should feel guilty about her death, and indeed directly culpable for it. I find it odd now that this gothic tendency should have existed so independently of any intention to end my life. Never for a moment did I research or consider any mode of suicide. I could very easily write a funeral oration in the morning and then try to secure an audition for “Annie” in the afternoon. (Teen-age me wanted to be the first black Annie. She did not understand that Annie is, at most, twelve.) But I was still very enamored of this funeral scenario. Skinny bitches with straight hair and straight teeth would hang their silky heads and weep with shame. People with parents who could afford contact lenses or even just non-N.H.S. spectacles would cower before my working-class posthumous righteousness. The sadistic French teacher who wouldn’t let me keep my Puffa jacket on in class would be forced to admit in front of everybody that being from Senegal was an unfair linguistic advantage that she had over her pupils, especially me. Comment dit-on la mort ? And Sasha would take back what she had said about “half-castes,” and the popular girls would notice my wit and inner beauty and want to hang, and my best friend would realize he was in love with me—and they would all be too late! Too late!

first_draft.candidate:
Every night, I'd curl up on my bed with my notebook, crafting elaborate funeral speeches, each one more detailed than the last. The scenario always started the same: my lifeless body at the front of the room, as if the world finally paused to consider me. The seats filled with faces ticked off a mental list—a gallery of those who underestimated or ignored me. I imagined my classmates, the ones with perfect hair and perfect lives, shifting uncomfortably on their pews. And there, among them, my French teacher, who never missed a chance to scold my accent, would sit with lips tightly pursed. I sketched scenes where my death forced a reevaluation, where those same people finally saw what was buried beneath my awkward stumbles and moments of invisibility.

Despite the morbid satisfaction it brought, these were never real plans, just fantasies of vindication. I didn't want to die; I just wanted them to see me. It was as if, through my absence, my presence could finally occupy space it wasn’t allowed in life. I wasn’t hoping to escape; I just wanted to be valued. April 16 began like any other day, but it ended with a sudden shift from imagination to reality. I wasn’t trying to cause a spectacle, wasn’t trying to bring about one of my own macabre scripts. Somehow, the window was open, the air still cool from an early spring, and then, just like that, I fell. It wasn’t elegant or dramatic but terrifying and surreal, a blur of sky and ground. When it happened, in those seconds suspended mid-air, I wasn’t thinking about speeches or guilt, just the shocking reality of gravity. Afterward, there were no fantasies left to write. It was all just bone and recovery, and the future blank and undecided as a fresh page.
